entries.title: Magnolia Bakery reopens week after health inspection found cockroaches, other violations
entries.summary: <p>Magnolia Bakery’s Chicago location has reopened this week after passing a follow-up health inspection Tuesday, days after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/07/15/magnolia-bakery-temporarily-closes-after-failing-a-health-inspection-that-found-cockroaches-other-violations" target="_blank" >the popular Loop bakery was closed</a> for health code violations, including pest-related issues.</p><p>The bakery, on the first floor of the Block 37 shopping mall at 108 N. State St., was categorized as “risk 1 (high)” following a failed health inspection July 13. Inspectors found live and dead cockroaches and “approximately 100 or more live small flies flying around” in prep areas, under sinks and inside storage cabinets, according to city data.</p><p>City health inspectors found 13 live cockroaches “crawling in between cracks and crevices” and “numerous” other dead cockroaches in the same areas, according to city data.</p><p>“The Magnolia Bakery team has been working nonstop on a corrective plan of action to reopen our doors,” a company spokesperson said in a statement. “We are pleased to report that we have reopened as of Tuesday, July 21 and have been thrilled to see so many of you again.”</p><p>Inspectors last week flagged other violations, including that the bakery’s hand-washing sinks were not properly supplied and accessible, and the staff bathroom sink drained too slowly. They also identified a gap along the bottom center of the bake shop’s street-side double doors that could allow more insects to get inside.</p><p>Inspectors also found that food debris had accumulated in food mixers, a walk-in cooler, storage shelves and on the exterior of a grease trap in the basement. Also noted were dust buildup from ceiling vents in the bathrooms and dining area.</p><p>The bakery was required to complete pest control measures and address the other violations before another city inspection could be conducted.</p><p>Block 37 is the bakery’s sole Chicago location. It opened in 2011 and is known for its creamy banana pudding and “Carrie” cupcakes, named after the “Sex and the City” character played by Sarah Jessica Parker.</p><p><i>Contributing: Ambar Colón</i></p>

entries.title: White Sox’ contending window opening just in time for Andrew Benintendi
entries.summary: <p>ARLINGTON, Texas — Ten years of MLB service time went by fast for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> outfielder Andrew Benintendi, for the most part.</p><p>“I remember coming up, guys saying, ‘Enjoy it, because it’s going to go fast,’” the veteran designated hitter said this week in the visitors’ clubhouse at Globe Life Field, a week after hitting the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/12/chicago-white-sox-mlb-draft-landon-thome-jim-thome-roch-cholowsky-andrew-benintendi-caleb-bonemer" target="_blank" ><u>career milestone</u></a> that locks up a fully vested pension.</p><p>“Maybe the last few years haven’t felt as fast,” the understated Benintendi said, nodding to his first three miserable seasons after signing the biggest free-agent contract in Sox history at five years and $75 million. “But it’s been good overall.”</p><p>And it’s getting better this season. After weathering the worst one in baseball history in 2024, enduring a brutal 324 losses over the first three years of his deal and falling far short of expectations, Benintendi has found a quietly productive groove while serving a lesser role than he envisioned when he arrived on the South Side.</p><p>The former Gold Glover barely ever plays the outfield anymore, was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/08/white-sox-andrew-benintendi-orioles-platton" target="_blank" ><u>platooned</u></a> at DH early in the year and often finds himself in the lower half of manager Will Venable’s batting order.</p><p>But a pair of RBI singles from Benintendi in Wednesday's 4-2 series-clinching win at Texas raised his RBI total to 52, third-highest on the team and well on pace to breaking his previous high with the Sox (64 in ‘24). His 16 two-baggers are fourth-most on the Sox, who moved a game ahead in the American League Central with the Guardians' loss. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Benny adds one more ✔️ <a href="https://t.co/iDQ32cdmP2">pic.twitter.com/iDQ32cdmP2</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://x.com/whitesox/status/2080110570292822514?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 23, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>With the upstart Sox playing their best baseball since 2021, Benintendi is enjoying the contending atmosphere he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/19/white-sox-andrew-benintendi-clubhouse-expectations" target="_blank" ><u>initially signed up for</u></a> — and having the most fun he’s had in years.</p><p>He's hitting .245/.306/.426, hardly overwhelming numbers alongside the breakout seasons of Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami and Colson Montgomery — but “they stand out to me,” Venable said.</p><p>“He’s made a huge impact. I feel like he’s coming through in these spots with his experience that he has," Venable said. "He’s been in these spots before and you know he’s got the ability and the demeanor to deal with them."</p><p>Benintendi’s line includes 10 home runs, plenty of them well-timed. His teammates are quick to point to his ninth-inning, three-run blast at Arizona on April 23 as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/23/munetaka-murakami-home-run-streak-andrew-benintendi-white-sox-win-arizona" target="_blank" ><u>a pivotal moment</u></a> for a squad that appeared headed for familiar struggles over the first few weeks of the season.</p><p>Then there was his eighth-inning, pinch-hit grand slam last month at Yankee Stadium providing <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/06/18/sean-burke-andrew-benintendi-white-sox-yankees-red-sox-junior-perez-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>another massive jolt</u></a> for a young team out to prove their stunning first-half success was no fluke.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Andrew Benintendi pinch-hit GRAND SLAM! <a href="https://t.co/2yUd9XkvrD">pic.twitter.com/2yUd9XkvrD</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2067780226520662095?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 19, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>All the better for Benintendi, who won a World Series with Boston in 2018, that a clubhouse full of young grinders are taking the reins.</p><p>“It helps a lot,” Benintendi said. “It seems if we get a few guys on, we can put up a lot of runs pretty quickly. It’s fun to be a part of this lineup.”</p><p>He’s the first one to point out that it’s the next generation powering their division race.</p><p>“The pitchers are giving us a good chance, they’re going out there pumping the zone and keeping the other team off-balanced, throwing up zeroes, limiting damage when they are getting baserunners.” Benintendi said. “They’re getting us back in the dugouts with bats in our hands. Clearly, we're a pretty streaky team when we get some guys on, so it's been good.”</p><p>The second-year manager Venable is grateful for the clubhouse counsel as well.</p><p>“It has meant a lot, a guy who has the experience and the wisdom of 10 years in the big leagues,” Venable said. “You also have a guy that’s creating a lot of space for these young players to be leaders and supporting them to advance in their careers, both in the clubhouse and on the field. He’s been a special addition for us.”</p>

entries.title: Drew Thorpe hopes to rejoin White Sox for playoff push after long road back to mound
entries.summary: <p>ARLINGTON, Texas — Drew Thorpe’s not a morning person, but he’ll make an exception if it means getting back to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> after two frustrating years of injury rehabilitation.</p><p>“Ten a.m. starts should be illegal, but I’ll take it,” Thorpe said, referring to his early first pitch in the desert last weekend with the Arizona Complex League Sox.</p><p>The right-hander threw two scoreless innings with three strikeouts in his biggest step yet back to the Sox since being <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/06/white-sox-right-hander-drew-thorpe-bullpen-session-dr-keith-meister-andrew-benintendi-everson-pereria-wikelman-gonzalez" target="_blank" ><u>sidelined</u></a> since July 31, 2024, with a slew of elbow issues, Tommy John surgery and an appendectomy to boot.</p><p>“It has been what feels like forever,” Thorpe said. “It was good to touch the mound again in somewhat of a game.”</p><p>Thorpe’s next step comes Friday with a three-inning outing at High-A Winston-Salem, and he hopes to ramp up from there — all the way back to the big leagues this season, he believes.</p><p>“I think so. That’s up to them,” Thorpe said, pointing to Sox leaders who acquired him in the Dylan Cease trade. Thorpe posted a 5.48 ERA but flashed tantalizing potential in nine starts for the Sox before going down.</p><p>“I’m in a really good spot right now,” he said. “Just have to build up. That’s how it goes. I’m ready to go.”</p><p>Manager Will Venable said a potential return for the Sox’ playoff push is “absolutely” possible.</p><p>“For him personally, just to be getting back healthy and active means a lot,” Venable said. “That’s the game plan, to push him and have him as somebody that can help us.”</p><h3>Quero returns</h3><p>Catcher Edgar Quero started Wednesday's rubber match in Texas, his first in the place of Kyle Teel, who <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/21/kyle-teel-injury-white-sox-catcher-edgar-quero" >could miss the rest of the regular season</a> with the ankle sprain he suffered Monday. Quero went 0-for-3 with a walk and an error after dropping a foul pop down the first-base line. He also got an ABS challenge wrong behind the plate. </p><p>Before the game, Quero said he felt sorry for his fellow backstop, but relished another big-league opportunity after struggling to a .486 OPS during Teel's first stint on the injured list.</p><p>"I started the season pretty bad," Quero said. "I have the chance right now to turn the page and do my stuff and get ready and help the team... I did everything I could in Triple-A to fix my swing and fix everything. I feel ready to go right now."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7c0000" name="image-7c0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/3dfebba/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3787x2125+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2F4f%2Fe245b79944ab9d01ad3fb5c28178%2F2287110002.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/31be404/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3787x2125+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2F4f%2Fe245b79944ab9d01ad3fb5c28178%2F2287110002.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4778970/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3787x2125+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2F4f%2Fe245b79944ab9d01ad3fb5c28178%2F2287110002.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="The White Sox' Noah Schultz pitches during the second inning against the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field Tuesday in Arlington, Texas. entries.title: 14-year-old e-bike rider killed in Wauconda crash
entries.summary: <p>A teen boy was killed after being hit by a car while riding an e-bike in Wauconda Tuesday, according to Wauconda police.</p><p>Tyler Waldal, 14, was riding the e-bike in the 500 block of Main Street at 9:58 p.m. when he was hit by an SUV, police said. He was taken to Advocate Condell Medical Center where he later died.</p><p>The crash remains under investigation.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Inter Miami beats Fire 3-2 to ruin MLS debut of Robert Lewandowski
entries.summary: <p>MIAMI — Preston Plambeck scored his first career goal in MLS in the 87th minute, Luis Suárez scored two goals, and Inter Miami beat the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire" >Fire</a> 3-2 on Wednesday night to spoil Robert Lewandowski's debut for the Fire.</p><p>Miami (10-2-4) has won five straight.</p><p>Suárez had his shot from the center of the area parried by goalkeeper Chris Brady but Plambeck slammed home the rebound.</p><p>The Fire took a 1-0 lead on an own goal by goalkeeper Rocco Ríos Novo in the 18th minute. Miami defender Ian Fray played the slow, rolling ball to Ríos Novo, but the ball slipped through the goalkeeper's legs as he whiffed on an attempted first-touch pass.</p><p>Suárez converted from the spot in the 27th to make it 1-1.</p><p>The 37-year-old Lewandowski signed with the Fire on June 29 and his first MLS appearance was delayed. The Fire had their game against Vancouver, which had originally been scheduled for Thursday, postponed until Oct. 6 due to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fire/2026/07/16/fire-robert-lewandowski-mls-debut-delayed-canadian-wildfires-postpones-match-vs-vancouver-whitecaps" >air quality conditions</a> in the Chicago area.</p><p>Lewandowski, a seven-time Bundesliga Golden Boot winner, scored a league-record 41 goals in the 2020-21 campaign with Bayern Munich.</p><p></p><p>The Fire (8-5-2) had its three-game win streak snapped.</p><p></p><p>Puso Dithejane subbed on for Philip Zinckernagel in the 62nd minute and scored his first career goal in MLS on a first-touch shot from just inside the penalty area to tie it 2-2 in the 67th.</p><p>Argentina internationals Lionel Messi and Rodrigo De Paul did not play for Miami following their World Cup final defeat to Spain on Sunday.</p><p>Hugo Cuypers, who currently leads MLS with 13 goals this season, will reportedly be leaving the Fire to join CF Monterrey of Liga MX.<br></p>
entries.author: AP

entries.title: Sydney Taylor is growing fast while the Sky repeat old mistakes
entries.summary: <p>Sydney Taylor walked off the court looking like she wanted to punch a wall.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> had just scrawled their frustrating signature all over Barclays Center. They played 35 excellent minutes, built a 12-point lead deep into the fourth quarter and gave it all back, losing on a Liberty free throw in the final second.</p><p>It is a troubling pattern that probably will keep the Sky from becoming a playoff team.</p><p>But a more encouraging one is emerging, too: Taylor keeps giving them chances to win.</p><p>The rookie scored a career-high 31 points Wednesday in a game with seven ties and 10 lead changes that really should have belonged to the Sky.</p><p>Not bad for a Long Island kid playing at Barclays Center for the first time. About 30 family members were in the stands, and she reminded them that she relishes the biggest stages.</p><p>She was nearly unstoppable in the first quarter. She buried a step-back three-pointer and outjumped 6'4 Liberty star Breanna Stewart to score in transition. After another silky midrange jumper, Liberty assistant Courtney Paris looked visibly frustrated, as if to ask: Why can't we stop her?</p><p>“She’s a hooper,” Liberty head coach Chris DeMarco said before the game. “She can score at all three levels. She plays not scared. She has really helped them.”</p><p>Quarters like that make the future feel immediate. Taylor can look like a finished product.</p><p>The second quarter offered the reminder that she is still a rookie. Her shot stopped falling, and she got scored on repeatedly.</p><p>“I think one of the bittersweet things about rookies that perform at such a high level early on is that you get caught up in all the things they do well that you forget to give them grace,” coach Tyler Marsh said before the game. “She still has learning curves that she’s going through.”</p><p>There are plenty. But there also has been obvious progress in the month since Taylor made her first start.</p><p>Taylor told the Sun-Times before Wednesday’s game that she feels more comfortable as a playmaker. She showed it with two smooth, one-handed feeds to center Kamilla Cardoso and finished with three assists.</p><p>After the red-hot start, Taylor's second-half was more measured. There were fewer flashy shots, but she got to the free-throw line and buried huge three-pointers.</p><p>Help came in the third quarter from a very different kind of rookie, Aicha Coulibaly, who doesn't score much but brings constant energy and activity — deflections, offensive rebounds and well-timed cuts.</p><p>Then, when the Liberty cut the Sky’s lead to one, the final handoff appeared to go to veteran point guard Courtney Vandersloot. She found Cardoso with a gorgeous pass, then hit a pull-up jumper to restore an eight-point lead with less than a minute left.</p><p>The general was going to make sure they finally pulled one out. Send them into the All-Star break with a little momentum. Keep their playoff hopes alive a little longer.</p><p>Until Liberty star Sabrina Ionescu hit two miracle three-pointers and drew a foul on another basket to complete the comeback.</p><p>“It felt like the Liberty made really big plays,” Vandersloot said after the game. “We were not perfect and we didn’t make enough plays but some of the shots that [Ionescu] hit, they just take the air out.”</p><p>The clutch loss mirrored Taylor’s first start against the Liberty a month earlier. Taylor hit a three-pointer in the final seconds to give the Sky the lead, only for Ionescu to answer with the winning layup.</p><p>Taylor has grown a lot since then — more comfortable creating for others and more certain that she belongs in moments like these.</p><p>The Sky, meanwhile, are still finding new ways to arrive at the same ending.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: Seeing one Cubs star in another: Pete Crow-Armstrong’s improved plate discipline earns Anthony Rizzo comp
entries.summary: <p><b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> catches everything.</p><p><b>Anthony Rizzo</b> can’t even reel in a home-run ball while holding a kid in the Wrigley Field bleachers.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Michael Busch hit a homer into the bleachers ...<br><br>Anthony Rizzo got the ball! <a href="https://t.co/oVp6EF54AE">pic.twitter.com/oVp6EF54AE</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2078548895517278445?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 18, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>All jokes aside — Rizzo was a Platinum Glove winner, after all — there is one thing manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> has noticed about his center fielder’s play this season that has him remembering the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ champion first baseman.</p><p>“One of the things he did is he moved up on the plate,” Counsell said while ruminating on Crow-Armstrong’s improved plate discipline and walk numbers. “I kind of equate that to Anthony Rizzo. Anthony Rizzo, at one point in his career, moved up on the plate, and then for most of his career, he was right on top of the plate, against left-handed pitching especially.</p><p>“It helped [Crow-Armstrong] better define the strike zone.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong’s improved on-base ability has been the talk of his MVP-caliber campaign to this point, a night-and-day difference from his breakout season a year ago. He started Wednesday with a .384 on-base percentage that ranked 13th in baseball.</p><p>After walking three times in Tuesday’s win, Crow-Armstrong was up to 52 walks on the season, in 101 games, a massive jump from the 29 walks he drew in 157 games last season.</p><p>“He’s a player that can <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/21/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-walk-triple-stolen-bases-defense-gold-glove-jed-hoyer-craig-counsell-matt-shaw-injury-ian-happ-all-time-home-run-list" >impact winning in so many different ways</a>,” second baseman <b>Nico Hoerner</b> said of Crow-Armstrong. “He doesn’t have to hit a home run to be the best player on the field that day. But he also can hit home runs and do that. He’s been amazing.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong’s walk rate has made an enormous leap from 4.5 percent last season to 11.8 percent this year. Rizzo was a prolific walker, too, with an 11-percent walk rate in his 10 seasons as a Cub, topping out at 13.2 percent in 2014.</p><p>“The rate at which it’s improved and how fast it’s improved, I don’t have any comparisons for it,” Counsell said. “I don’t have any explanations for it. It’s a great athlete coming into his own as a great player.</p><p>“This is a young, great athlete getting more experience, and it’s that take-off that you hope you see.”</p><h3><b>Reunited, will it feel so good?</b></h3><p><b>Aaron Civale</b> is back with the Cubs after a weekend trade with the A’s, reuniting the righty pitcher with the team he pitched for during the postseason last year.</p><p>Civale, who put up a 2.08 ERA in five regular-season relief appearances, logged 4 1/3 scoreless innings in Game 1 of the NLDS.</p><p>He’s a Cub once more as the team continues to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/21/cubs-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-tarik-skubal-rumors-pitching-injuries-bullpen-trent-thornton-phil-maton" >seek aid for an injury-ravaged pitching staff</a>, hoping he can deliver the types of results he did last year and not the 5.42 ERA he had with the A’s.</p><p>“It feels good to be back, it doesn’t feel like too long ago,” Civale said Wednesday. “We’re trying out a few new things, locations on the mound. We’re just trying to get things back feeling good and making sure that I’m out there competing the best that I can. I’m just trying to learn from each thing.”</p><p>Civale pitched 2⅓ innings in relief Tuesday, giving up two runs on four hits and a couple walks.</p><h3><b>Seiya slugs, but nothing more for Cubs’ bats</b></h3><p>Right fielder <b>Seiya Suzuki</b> extended his on-base streak to 11 games with his first-inning homer in Wednesday’s 5-1 loss. He’s hitting .341 in that span.</p><p>The Cubs’ lineup managed just four hits and a walk on the night, with only two of those hits coming after the first inning, a far cry from the 11 hits and 11 walks they had a night prior.</p><p>“Maybe we wasted all our hits last night,” Crow-Armstrong said.</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-c90005" name="list-c90005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageCount=4704, pageNumber=1, titleUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, title=Latest on the Cubs, bodyFont=font-3, showListNumbers=false, imagePositionHorizontal=null, rteBodyFont=font-3, headerBottomBorderColor=#111010, subTitle=null, stickyHeader=true, listTitleColor=#000000, items=[{type=Image, categoryUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs, description=[{items=[There are different levels of buying and selling at the trade deadline. entries.title: Dear Abby: Boyfriend suddenly sings a different tune about children
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My boyfriend, "Adam," and I have been together for four years. We are very much in love and share similar views on most things. We agree that a marriage license is just a piece of paper and our relationship is already a marriage, so we don't need one.</p><p>We have also discussed the idea of having children in the future, and we agreed we didn't want any. I have never had the drive to be a mother, although I have been told I would make an excellent one. Even Adam has said it. But we both have been adamant that we don't want children. We love our freedom way too much (or at least I do), not to mention the finances involved, and we want to travel a lot.</p><p>Because I can no longer take birth control, I have been considering tying my tubes. Adam volunteered to get a vasectomy because he said he doesn't want me to go in for surgery. Well, this week he confessed that he hasn't gone through with it because he's scared and he still might want a baby.</p><p>Adam has flip-flopped back and forth over the last two years about having or not having a child, while I have stayed firm on not wanting any. Should I consider having a child if that's what he wants? I love him. He's the man I see myself growing old with, and I don't want to break his heart. — <i>PERPLEXED IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR PERPLEXED:</b> Parenthood is a joy that should be embarked upon because you sincerely want a child, not to please your boyfriend. The truth is that motherhood is a lifetime responsibility. It doesn't end when the child turns 21. I implore you not to make such an important decision to please anyone but yourself, because if something happened to Adam, you would have to raise that child alone.</p><p>There are other options besides birth control medications you should discuss with your doctor. Unless you are absolutely certain you want to become a mother, you should utilize them religiously.</p><p>As to a marriage license "just being a piece of paper," let me point out that it is much more than that. It entitles a spouse to participate in medical decisions if a husband or wife becomes incapacitated, and it also guarantees rights of inheritance if, heaven forbid, something should happen to either of you. Yes, I know there is such a thing as common law marriage, but a marriage certificate is better — trust me on that.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> We have a morbidly obese 30-year-old grandson (at least 300 pounds) coming for dinner along with family. We don't have any chairs that will accommodate him. We are concerned that he will be embarrassed. Can you help us in handling this dilemma? — <i>HOSTESS IN CALIFORNIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR HOSTESS:</b> I'll try. Go online or start calling around to furniture rental companies or catering companies that may have chairs you can rent that will accommodate your grandson. If that isn't an option, consider buying something sturdy, perhaps from a secondhand or thrift store, to have available for him during family gatherings.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>Good advice for everyone — teens to seniors — is in "The Anger in All of Us and How to Deal With It." To order, send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds), to: Dear Abby, Anger Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: U.S. can't retreat from Iran without any wins
entries.summary: <p>While President Donald Trump threatens to destroy “ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT” in Iran for every shot they take at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, Americans back home are hoping and praying this folly of a war wraps up yesterday.</p><p>Strikes over the weekend brought the death toll for U.S. troops to 18, with 100 more injured. The Strait of Hormuz is essentially closed again, with Iran’s Houthi allies in Yemen threatening to block other oil routes. Gas prices are up 16 cents from the average a week ago, 88 cents higher than last year and $1.04 higher than the week before the war, <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/21/donald-trump-iran-war-midterms-01006721" target="_blank" >per Politico</a>. And Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth admitted in a hearing Tuesday that the conflict had already cost U.S. taxpayers $37.5 billion — as <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/07/22/politics/iran-price-tag-no-answers-how-it-ends?cid=ios_app&source=sub_web_wall-exc" target="_blank" >he asked</a> for $67 billion more.</p><p>All of this while no one — not Hegseth, not Trump, not Secretary of State Marco Rubio or Vice President JD Vance — can tell voters how or when we plan to exit this war having achieved anything of long-term significance. It’s the very definition of a quagmire.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f90000" name="module-f90000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Meanwhile, Iran and its dangerous proxies are clearly playing the long game, hoping that upcoming American midterm elections force the U.S. to exit the war we started without accomplishing a single one of our stated objectives — a very real possibility.</p><p>Trump is posturing, as he’s wont to do, insisting he’s not influenced by the calendar. </p><p>“I don’t view it as ‘Gee, we’re having an election in a period of time,’ ” he said Tuesday. “No, the election — I can’t think about that having to do with this. I think people are very impressed.”</p><p>Not so, as a <a class="Link" href="https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/55176-maga-republicans-still-support-iran-war-but-most-americans-say-it-was-wrong-decision-july-10-13-2026-economist-yougov-poll" target="_blank" >majority</a> of Americans now say the war in Iran was the wrong decision, while <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/07/22/poll-maga-souring-iran-war-costs-trump-01006976" target="_blank" >a belief</a> that the war is worth the economic cost among Trump’s MAGA base has dropped to just over a third — a 13 point drop in two months.</p><p>Voters, Republican lawmakers up for reelection and the Iranian regime — all united in their hope that Trump can be pushed to the exits by the election politics of an unpopular war.</p><p>But for once, I hope Trump isn’t bluffing.</p><p>We shouldn’t have entered this war, and we most definitely shouldn’t have entered it without a clear strategy. But here we are, and it’s now our job to leave it responsibly.</p><p>What does that mean?</p><p>Unfortunately, it means admitting we likely can’t make good on a number of the grandiose promises Trump made to justify the war in the first place. It seems we’ve given up on the idea of regime change and liberating the Iranian people, to name two. But we can and should pursue other objectives that would leave the U.S., our allies and the region better off.</p><p>First and foremost, we must leave with verifiable restraints on and multilateral monitoring of Iran’s nuclear program. If it’s unrealistic or costly to retrieve Iran’s buried uranium cache, we must secure a non-conditional non-proliferation agreement — with teeth.</p><p>We must leave having guaranteed unfettered access to shipping routes, from the Strait of Hormuz to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Our European, Asian and Gulf allies must be integrated into a joint coalition to protect international shipping lanes from repeated extortion attempts.</p><p>And we must leave our regional allies, like Kuwait, protected from retaliatory strikes through binding nonaggression commitments and a long-term offshore carrier strike group presence to prevent a security vacuum.</p><p>This is a far cry from what Trump promised with his ill-advised and ill-prepared blunder of a war — and in the case of Hormuz, it’s merely restoring access we already had before the war. But it’s the least we should accept in our retreat.</p><p>As much as we want to get out now, we owe it to our allies, our Gulf partners, our troops — and the Iranian people — to leave this mess of our own making with something to show for it.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-db0000" name="module-db0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Trump, once again, threatens TV stations. Will FCC chief follow through?
entries.summary: <p>Imagine how Republicans would react if a Democratic president reflexively threatened to yank the broadcast licenses of TV stations because he did not like their news coverage or programming decisions. President Donald Trump has been <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/01/18/how-the-fcc-became-the-speech-police/" target="_blank" >doing that</a> since his first term, and he <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/07/17/trump-threatens-to-revoke-abc-and-nbc-licenses-for-not-broadcasting-his-election-speech/" target="_blank" >did it again</a> last week after ABC and NBC declined to offer live coverage of his <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2026/07/politics/annotated-transcript-trump-speech-us-election-vis/" target="_blank" >speech</a> about election security.</p><p>These threats are part of an intimidation campaign that has already yielded striking concessions to Trump's whims. His weaponization of the Federal Communications Commission is designed to chill constitutionally protected speech, establishing a precedent that Republicans may <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/09/24/trumps-vision-of-broadcast-regulation-is-a-threat-to-conservatives/" target="_blank" >regret</a> when their opponents take control of the White House.</p><p>Brendan Carr, the Trump-appointed FCC chairperson, seems to think broadcasters have a legal obligation to please the president. "Broadcasters must operate in the public interest," Carr <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/BrendanCarrFCC/status/2032855414233047172" target="_blank" >declared</a> in March, "and they will lose their licenses if they do not."</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-560000" name="module-560000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p>As Carr understands it, "the public interest" requires broadcasters to <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/07/25/the-fccs-paramount-skydance-decision-aims-to-reshape-broadcast-journalism-by-bureaucratic-fiat/" target="_blank" >cover</a> the president "fully, accurately, and fairly." It may also require them to eschew <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/BrendanCarrFCC/status/2032855414233047172" target="_blank" >war reporting</a> that embarrasses the president and <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/06/trumps-responses-to-kimmel-and-comey-highlight-his-disregard-for-freedom-of-speech/" target="_blank" >punish</a> late-night comedians whose jokes offend him.</p><p>Any attempt to impose such a vague, open-ended standard on speakers in other media would be plainly unconstitutional. But broadcasters are different, Carr <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/BrendanCarrFCC/status/2032855414233047172" target="_blank" >avers</a>, because "the American people have subsidized [them] to the tune of billions of dollars by providing free access to the nation's airwaves."</p><p>Trump echoed that rationale for speech regulation last week, when he <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2026/07/politics/annotated-transcript-trump-speech-us-election-vis/" target="_blank" >said</a> broadcasters "use our public, multibillion-dollar-in-value airways for absolutely no money." But that is plainly not true, since broadcast licenses <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/03/16/brendan-carr-says-he-can-police-tv-journalism-because-broadcast-licenses-are-free/" target="_blank" >figure in the prices</a> that media companies pay when they acquire TV or radio stations.</p><p>Trump nevertheless relied on that false premise in <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2026/07/politics/annotated-transcript-trump-speech-us-election-vis/" target="_blank" >arguing</a> that the failure of ABC and NBC to give his speech the attention he thought it deserved "should mean a revocation of their licenses." Whether or not Carr follows through on that suggestion, he has made it clear that he views correcting anti-Trump bias as an important part of his job.</p><p>That understanding of the FCC's mission explains why Carr <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/03/14/the-fccs-show-trial-against-cbs-is-a-political-power-play/" target="_blank" >seriously entertained</a> the possibility that CBS committed "broadcast news distortion" by editing a preelection interview with Kamala Harris in a way that made her seem <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/02/06/trump-is-flat-out-lying-about-the-60-minutes-interview-with-harris/" target="_blank" >slightly more cogent</a>. It explains why Carr <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/07/25/the-fccs-paramount-skydance-decision-aims-to-reshape-broadcast-journalism-by-bureaucratic-fiat/" target="_blank" >bragged</a> about requiring changes to journalistic practices at CBS as a condition for approving Skydance Media's acquisition of Paramount, the network's parent company.</p><p>Carr's <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/09/23/brendan-carr-says-networks-must-serve-the-public-interest-what-does-that-mean/" target="_blank" >conception</a> of "the public interest" was also at the root of his most flagrant attempt to exert control over broadcast content: the <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/09/18/brendan-carr-flagrantly-abused-his-powers-to-cancel-jimmy-kimmel/" target="_blank" >regulatory threats</a> that preceded ABC's suspension of" Jimmy Kimmel Live" last September. It likewise underlies his <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/01/23/the-fcc-wants-to-police-how-many-conservatives-appear-on-the-view/" target="_blank" >warning</a> that talk shows like "The View" can no longer rely on their <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2026/05/11/brendan-carrs-equal-time-threat-against-the-view-is-blatantly-unconstitutional-abc-says/" target="_blank" >longstanding exemption</a> from the "equal time" rule — a change that would effectively prohibit them from interviewing political candidates.</p><p>So far, Carr has not delivered on Trump's oft-repeated <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/11/19/a-reporters-unwelcome-questions-provoke-yet-another-trump-threat-to-yank-broadcast-licenses/" target="_blank" >threats</a> to revoke broadcast licenses. But in April, he <a class="Link" href="https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DA-26-416A1.pdf" target="_blank" >announced</a> an early review of ABC's licenses, ostensibly because of concerns about "unlawful discrimination."</p><p>Actual license revocations are not necessary to cow broadcasters, as illustrated by what happened after Trump filed a <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/07/02/by-settling-trumps-laughable-lawsuit-against-cbs-paramount-strikes-a-blow-at-freedom-of-the-press/" target="_blank" >ludicrous lawsuit</a> alleging that the Harris interview qualified as consumer fraud under Texas and federal law. Although CBS accurately <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/a-statement-from-60-minutes/" target="_blank" >noted</a> that Trump's complaint was "completely without merit" and vowed to "vigorously defend against it," Paramount ultimately <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/07/02/by-settling-trumps-laughable-lawsuit-against-cbs-paramount-strikes-a-blow-at-freedom-of-the-press/" target="_blank" >agreed</a> to a $16 million settlement.</p><p>That decision followed Trump's <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2024/10/28/trump-thinks-news-outlets-should-lose-their-broadcast-licenses-even-when-they-have-none/" target="_blank" >threats</a> to revoke the network's broadcast licenses and Carr's <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/02/05/how-the-fccs-warrior-for-free-speech-became-our-censor-in-chief/" target="_blank" >initiation</a> of the "news distortion" investigation. It came as the FCC was deciding whether to allow the Paramount/Skydance merger, which it finally <a class="Link" href="https://reason.com/2025/07/25/the-fccs-paramount-skydance-decision-aims-to-reshape-broadcast-journalism-by-bureaucratic-fiat/" target="_blank" >approved</a> a few weeks later based on the expectation of a Trump-friendlier CBS News.</p><p>That episode showed how easily "the public interest" can be conflated with the president's personal interests. It's a lesson that Republicans should take to heart if they allow for the possibility that they will not always control these levers of power.</p><p><i>Jacob Sullum is a senior editor at Reason magazine.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-ef0000" name="module-ef0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: All-star Chicago musicians to perform night of protest songs
entries.summary: <p>Public disapproval over federal agents in the streets, the war in Iran, rising grocery and fuel prices and corruption at the highest levels of government led Dave Specter to organize. For the Chicago blues guitarist, that meant working the phone to invite musicians from throughout the city to stand onstage with him Sunday to sing songs of resistance.</p><p>“It’s our responsibility as musicians. This is what America’s about,” he said. “Protest music has always been a part of the need to stand up against injustice and speak out.”</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> target="_blank" >Privacy Policy</a></p> </div> </form> </bsp-form> </div> </div><p>Specter’s efforts resulted in “Songs of Protest, Sounds of Freedom,” on July 26 at Space in Evanston. The evening will feature just what the title promises across a spectrum of Chicago music, from blues artists Billy Branch, Melody Angel and John Katke, to jazz singer Lynne Jordan, slam poet Marc Smith and punk songwriter Jason Narducy. Also on the lineup are rock auteur Nicholas Tremulis, singer-songwriter Steve Dawson, pop singer Phil Angotti and reggae singer Kwame Bediako. Proceeds from the show benefit the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights.</p><p>Chicago musicians have long played a pivotal role in political and social movements, from the Staple Singers and Curtis Mayfield providing the soundtrack to Civil Rights activism to folk-rock songwriter Michael McDermott <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/music/2025/10/18/chicago-singer-songwriter-releases-new-song-ahead-of-no-kings-protest" target="_blank" ><u>releasing a song</u></a> to commemorate the first “No Kings” march last year. More recently, musicians like Bruce Springsteen, Dessa, Dropkick Murphys, and Billy Bragg have used songs to express a range of emotions, from anguish to defiance.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b60000" name="module-b60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>“Songs of Protest, Sounds of Freedom”</h3><b>When</b>: July 26<br><b>Where</b>: Evanston Space, 1245 N. Chicago Ave.<br><b>Ticket info</b>: Tickets from $25; <a class="Link" href="http://evanstonspace.com" target="_blank" ><u>evanstonspacemusic.com</u></a></div> </div><p>Locally, Specter, who is a partner in Space, released several protest songs over the years; most recently “The Times are Deranging (The Buck Stops Where?),” a slow blues number that blasts the current White House inhabitant. “Can’t stop lying/good people are dying/fools believe that he really cares,” Specter sings.</p><p>He said his political outlook was shaped by his father, Jerry Specter, a community organizer who in the 1970s helped lead resistance against the former Mayor Richard J. Daley administration’s plan to transform the former Municipal Tuberculosis Sanitarium on the Northwest Side into a commercial shopping center.</p><p>Today, the site is North Park Village, consisting of a nature center, senior housing and other neighborhood facilities. “He taught me that when you’re confronted with a bully, you stand up and you fight,” said Specter. “I don’t think passivism is particularly effective in times like this.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-790000" The club provided the entire room for two separate drives that totaled more than 7,000 postcards.</p><p>“When you have a venue that provides an amazing experience for musicians and audience members but also embraces activism, I’ll do anything I can do be part of what Dave is doing,” Narducy said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-fa0000" name="image-fa0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/caa0854/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F6d%2F695688bc48d09053204d80b281bc%2F20220602-melody-angel-mm00200.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7134ff2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F6d%2F695688bc48d09053204d80b281bc%2F20220602-melody-angel-mm00200.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bf8f079/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F6d%2F695688bc48d09053204d80b281bc%2F20220602-melody-angel-mm00200.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Melody Angel and her band is rehearsing for the Blues Fest at the Music Garage Room in 2022. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bf8f079/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F6d%2F695688bc48d09053204d80b281bc%2F20220602-melody-angel-mm00200.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bc01083/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F6d%2F695688bc48d09053204d80b281bc%2F20220602-melody-angel-mm00200.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bf8f079/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2500x1403+0+132/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe1%2F6d%2F695688bc48d09053204d80b281bc%2F20220602-melody-angel-mm00200.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Singer and guitarist Melody Angel is among the musicians performing at “Songs of Protest, Sounds of Freedom.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Events like “Songs of Protest, Sounds of Freedom,” he said, are not about convincing people to change their vote. Their greatest value is about “building community and building community is the way you create change in politics.”</p><p>“It’s important to not feel alone. That’s what the best music does anyway,” Narducy said. “When people hear someone sing, it’s a reminder that ‘Oh yeah, I’m not crazy for what I believe in.’”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-be0000" name="html-embed-module-be0000"></a><iframe data-testid="embed-iframe" style="border-radius:12px" src="https://open.spotify.com/embed/playlist/207evvpzfkuY60HAQDKRoz?utm_source=generator&si=dd17a600a5e64ee4" width="100%" height="352" frameBorder="0" allowfullscreen="" allow="autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; fullscreen; picture-in-picture" loading="lazy"></iframe> </div> </div><p>Specter said inspiration for the show was “Songs of Conscience, Sounds of Freedom,” a show documenting the role music has played in protest movements over the years that ran at the Woody Guthrie Center Tulsa and the Grammy Museum in Los Angeles. Among the instruments and handwritten lyrics from Guthrie, Springsteen, Pete Seeger, Josh White, and others, are lyrics Specter wrote for “The Ballad of George Floyd,” a song he and Chicago blues harp player Billy Branch released in 2020. “It was a total honor,” Specter said.</p><p>Each performer at the Space event will perform two songs, including originals and protest songs that span decades. “As a musician, it is more effective to speak through our music than to get into an argument on social media or in a bar,” Specter said. “Music brings people together. That’s what art should do.”</p>

entries.title: Inside Lithuania's defense strategy against Russia
entries.summary: <p>KYBARTAI AND VILNIUS, Lithuania — Rimas Rimkus is patching some asphalt at the end of his driveway on a narrow lane off the main drag of J. Basanavičiaus Street in the town of Kybartai.</p><p>He invites visitors into his fenced backyard, adorned with a decorative wishing well, swinging love seat, mini greenhouse and rows of young strawberry plants. </p><p>His adult son, Danielius, joins him as he unlocks the high fence's back gate to show what's next-door.</p><p>Russia.</p><p>Just beyond a small field is a border post in Kaliningrad, a 5,800-square-mile piece of Russia that's home to 1 million Russians and possibly 100 tactical nuclear warheads.</p><p>Though it was a peaceful April morning, other times the father and son say the air is filled with the sound of rifle shots. Sometimes their house shakes from a detonation.</p><p>Lithuania also has a 422-mile border with Russia's ally Belarus, from which Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.</p><p>Lithuanians call this area their "dangerous neighborhood."</p><p>"If war starts, I think we'd all be bombarded," Danielius Rimkus says. "It’s their decision if they want war or not. We’re just here waiting."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" data-align-center> <a class="AnchorLink" They want Americans to support it, too.</p><p>President Donald Trump has made numerous threats to pull out of the alliance, even though Lithuania has pledged to spend nearly 5.4% of its gross domestic product on defense this year, the highest percentage in Europe.</p><p>Romas Šunokas, 65, Kybartai’s town administrator, has lived in the area his entire life. Šunokas supports NATO and the Lithuanian government’s moves to strengthen its borders.</p><p>"I hope that the Russian side will see that Lithuanians are preparing," he says through a translator.</p><p>While he prefers to stay out of politics and focus on local constituent concerns, Šunokas knows that NATO’s Article 5 — which says an attack against one member is an attack against all — provides protection for Lithuania.</p><p>At the same time, he says Kybartai is doing its own work to prepare, like teaching schoolchildren about drones and holding evacuation drills.</p><p>"We are connected with this land, and we will protect it because this is where we grew up, this is where we are raising our children. also important because of the Suwalki Gap, a 65-mile strip of land that's the border between Lithuania and its NATO ally Poland. </p><p>The gap, with Kaliningrad to the west and Belarus to the east, is the Achilles' heel of NATO. It's where the West believes Russian President Vladimir Putin would go if he were to militarily test NATO. By controlling the gap, Russia could prevent NATO land troops from reaching Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia.</p><p>Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys says Lithuania is trying to create enough of a deterrence that Putin never gets that far.</p><p>"The effective deterrence will be when the troops will be at the very front line, when they will be visible to Russians and to their allies, the Belarussians, and there will be no doubt that they would be employed from the very first minute if our defense requires it," he says.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-fc0000" name="html-embed-module-fc0000"></a><div style="min-height:316px" id="datawrapper-vis-DXY81"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/DXY81/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-DXY81"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/DXY81/full.png" alt="Locator map" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Lithuania has invited 5,000 German soldiers to stay permanently by 2027 and has regularly hosted about 1,000 U.S. troops, though the size and timing of the next U.S. rotation is under review. Lithuania has 23,000 active-duty armed forces and an extensive civil defense infrastructure.</p><p>At a NATO summit in July, most European leaders tiptoed around Trump, who has repeatedly threatened to invade NATO territory Greenland and complained that Europe should be funding more of its own defense.</p><p>Budrys says the silver lining to Trump’s disparagement of NATO is that other European countries are spending more on defense.</p><p>"We are so grateful for the United States, keeping their forces in Lithuania and other Baltic states," Budrys says. the Seimas, voted in the spring to establish a military training ground on 56 square miles of forested land near Kapčiamiestis, close to the Belarussian end of the Suwalki Gap. Military drills are expected to begin in 2028, and the site will be able to accommodate 3,500 to 4,000 troops, mostly Lithuanian forces.</p><p>Civilians are also stepping up. More than 19,000 men and women have joined the Lithuanian Riflemen's Union, a group founded in 1919 and reestablished after the country's independence to help with disaster relief and community resilience. They get training in drones, cyber defense, medical support, logistics and engineering to assist the armed forces if needed.</p><p>Lithuania's goal, defense experts say, is to repel an invasion for 10 to 15 days until NATO troops could arrive.</p><p>NATO tensions hover over people at a Sunday flea market in Kalvarija, a short distance from the Suwalki Gap.</p><p>Seller Jūratė Maksimavičienė, 61, says she hopes NATO doesn’t crumble.</p><p>"I’m afraid for the future of NATO and Trump deciding to leave," she says. "It would be good if they vote Trump out. Only Americans can do that. Ukraine</h3><p>The lessons from nearby Ukraine are obvious, and the country's blue-and-yellow flag flies everywhere in Lithuania.</p><p>"We know what they [Russians] do in occupied territories," says Žygimantas Pavilionis, a member of parliament for the center-right Homeland Union party, who was Lithuania's ambassador to the U.S. and Mexico from 2010 to 2015.</p><p>Pavilionis says while he's dismayed by the Trump administration's friendliness toward Russia and Belarus, he hopes the U.S. never pulls its support from NATO and Lithuania.</p><p>He called Lithuanians "the Americans of the East," standing for democratic values at a time of rising authoritarianism. The country has sent troops to U.S.-run wars in Iraq and Afghanistan and has offered to help stabilize the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/06/11/spiking-gas-prices-chicagoans-stop-rising-food-prices-inflation" >Strait of Hormuz</a>.</p><p>Pavilionis wants Ukraine to win, then share its military expertise to "show very clearly to the Russians, 'Don’t even start to move.'"</p><p>Ukraine recently signed an agreement with Lithuania to launch a joint defense program to develop new military technologies, like the drones Ukraine has become known for.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a channel Laisvės TV ("Freedom TV"), has helped crowdfund assistance for Ukraine since 2022.</p><p>The fight is personal for Tapinas, 49, whose grandmother was exiled to Siberia by the Soviets with his mother, then a 1-year-old.</p><p>His father, Laimonas Tapinas, was chairman of the board of Lithuanian Radio and Television in January 1991, when Soviet troops stormed newly independent Lithuania and seized the public broadcaster's offices.</p><p>Tapinas remembers his dad coming home — injured after a Soviet soldier bashed him with a rifle — getting first aid and heading back out to help.</p><p>"I think that pretty much sums up why we are, and I like to be, among the first who would like to help Ukraine," he says.</p><p>"I’m quite envious of Americans because you take liberty for granted. We cannot take our liberty for granted. And we need to know that the price of freedom in our country is eternal vigilance. It’s been like that for 300 years."</p><p>The threats can feel relentless and some don't involve tanks or troops. Lithuania's President Gitanas Nausėda last week said intelligence assessments point to Russia planning potential attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltic countries or Poland.</p><p>Belarus has sent thousands of migrants from the Middle East and North Africa — with false promises of jobs in the EU — to Lithuania, beginning in 2021. The aim was to destabilize Lithuania, which had to scramble to secure its border. </p><p>People in Belarus also launched hundreds of mysterious weather balloons into Lithuania last year. The balloons forced the closure of Vilnius' airport more than two dozen times.</p><p>And an undersea telecommunications cable between Lithuania and Sweden was severed in 2024, an incident that raised questions about foreign involvement.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-fullBleed> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ad0000" name="image-ad0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/68b29eb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7621x4277+0+403/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F4a%2Fec7049e24323aaea776285ec8d36%2Flithuania-06xx26-126.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a16e8b1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7621x4277+0+403/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F4a%2Fec7049e24323aaea776285ec8d36%2Flithuania-06xx26-126.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5f27493/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7621x4277+0+403/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F4a%2Fec7049e24323aaea776285ec8d36%2Flithuania-06xx26-126.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of the National Crisis Information Centre in Vilnius, discusses a map of documented migrant crossings from Belarus into Lithuania on April 21. The center, created in 2023, is tasked with identifying threats and coordinating responses.</p><p>Operating from a Soviet-era government building, the center monitors Lithuania's border using video surveillance, seismic sensors and drones. The data is analyzed using software by Palantir Technologies.</p><p>"We can detect steps when somebody is approaching the border," Vitkauskas says.</p><p>Lithuania is pushing an internal concept of "total defense," which means everyone plans for the unthinkable.</p><p>Public buildings have signs marking underground shelters, and new construction projects include safe spaces. Schools teach children how to recognize disinformation campaigns on social media, and businesses plan for continuity in an emergency.</p><p>"Every citizen needs to feel their role and part in our national defense," Vitkauskas says. "It’s not just thinking of being able to shoot or use a weapon in order to defend your country, but are there other duties that people have to take care of? You know, take care of your family, your neighbors, how to prepare resources in order to help your military to fight the enemies."</p><p>He says Lithuania wants preparation, not panic.</p><p>"We don't necessarily think that there will be a full-scale military invasion and occupation as such. It could be something in between," he says.</p><p>Foreign sabotage often happens via screens, propaganda expert Vytautas Matulevičius says.</p><p>Lithuanians are good at spotting disinformation, but he says they aren't immune to a "fear offensive" campaign that tries to make them feel unprotected.</p><p>"Russia is waging cognitive warfare against us to achieve its political goals," Matulevičius says. "Division of the West, division between the states of the alliance — NATO or European Union — in order that we fight with each other and forget who the real adversary is."</p><p>Countering that strategy on TikTok, Instagram, Telegram and other platforms is a priority for Lithuania and other frontline NATO countries. European law allows governments to act against blatant digital disinformation, violent speech or banned symbols.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> Repsense uses artificial intelligence to monitor and analyze social media videos to see what's being pushed by disinformation accounts. The company's clients include the Lithuanian government, the European Parliament and other government and private entities.</p><p>Malign narratives often start on social media, then bubble up to podcasters and mainstream media, Liudvikas Andriulis, chief commercial officer at Repsense, says.</p><p>In September, Repsense deployed its technology during Moldova's parliamentary elections to help authorities identify and take down nearly half a million Russian accounts that were disseminating propaganda, pushing false messages like Moldova is overrun by gay foreigners or it's doomed to poverty, Andriulis says.</p><p>He says videos encouraging people to feel hopeless about voting or that lie about news events are most concerning, and it's a lesson for Americans.</p><p>"No one wants their elections to be interfered with," he says. "On both sides of the Atlantic, we understand that election integrity, the democratic process, the ability to choose and win elections fair and square is very important. The problem now is that TikTok is basically placing a TV in everyone's head."</p><p>Vitkauskas says the Lithuanian government's response to propaganda depends on the content, source and context. </p><p>If the narrative misses the mark, the response is nothing. If disinformation is percolating online, the center might flag it for academicians or journalists to debunk. If it's taking hold, government institutions might step up and publicly react.</p><p>"If it’s a really significant incident, we might have even our state officials at the highest level, whether it will be the prime minister or president or speaker of the parliament, address the issue and explain to the population what has happened," he says.</p><p>Vitkauskas says Lithuanian schools also teach students critical thinking.</p><p>"If you are informed and you prepare," he says, "it means that you are safe."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-fullBleed> <div class="Enhancement-item" Longworth Media fellows. Yet the country of 2.8 million people is located at one of Europe’s most vulnerable spots for military defense.<br><br>Zimmermann interviewed more than 50 people for the six-story series, from a former president and a current foreign minister to ordinary Lithuanians living at a time of both promise and peril.<br><br><h4>Coming soon</h4><ul id="rte-0349c372-861f-11f1-a8e9-dd50cc1b3f33"><li><b>Thursday</b>: Why most Lithuanians support NATO and what Lithuania is doing to protect itself from threats</li><li><b>Friday</b>: Chicago and Lithuania are linked in their love of basketball</li><li><b>Saturday</b>: An interview with former President Valdas Adamkus</li><li><b>Sunday</b>: From furniture-making to tech, Lithuania’s economy is thriving, with six unicorn companies</li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Secrecy over sex abuse permeates traditionalist Catholic group whose leaders were excommunicated by Pope Leo
entries.summary: <p>A controversial “fraternity” of priests whose leaders were recently excommunicated by Pope Leo XIV — and that maintains a quiet presence in the Chicago area with a church in west suburban Oak Park and a priory on the Northwest Side — fashions itself as an authentic practitioner of Catholicism.</p><p>But the Society of Saint Pius X, perhaps known best for embracing the old Latin mass and other practices and beliefs often described as “traditionalist” or “conservative,” shares an unfortunate characteristic with many of the more mainstream Catholic religious orders: a history of alleged child sexual abuse.</p><p>While some of the troubles are known publicly — including in France where the media has reported on a priest from the society who was sentenced to 20 years in prison in 2023 for sexual misconduct against 27 minors — it’s unclear how widespread they’ve been within the international organization, often referred to as SSPX.</p><p>The group’s website decries the scourge of sexual abuse, saying it’s “concerned with the safety of all those who are members and guests of our various organizations and institutions. We are completely committed to protecting the safety of everyone who attends our chapels, schools, camps, outings, or events. Abuse of any kind is never to be tolerated under any circumstance.”</p><p>But the SSPX website doesn’t maintain a public list of credibly accused members in the United States like many religious orders currently in good standing, from the Augustinians, to which Pope Leo belongs, to the Carmelites, Dominicans and Jesuits, to which the late Pope Francis belonged.</p><p> SSPX leaders wouldn't provide names or a tally of their alleged offenders when asked by the Chicago Sun-Times.</p><p>Many victims of the church’s decades-old abuse crisis say they support public disclosure of credibly accused clergy through church-based sex offender registries as a means of healing, and of ensuring better accountability from the church that was once much more mired in secrecy on this subject.</p><p>But popes have left the handling of such disclosures up to individual dioceses, which are church jurisdictions helmed by a bishop and based on geography, and individual religious orders, which usually follow in the mold of a saint and have their own leaders. SSPX is not technically a religious order — and even before the latest crisis it carried an “irregular” status within the broader church — but has similarities.</p><div class="Enhancement" leaders.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Fabrice Coffrini / AFP via Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Italian sociologist Massimo Introvigne, who has studied the group, says: “They have had some cases of sex abuses but not more than other Catholic groups. Unlike in the mainline Roman Catholic Church, discussing sex abuse is not one of their priorities.”</p><p>SSPX leaders gave the Sun-Times a written statement saying it “does not give responses to the media on these questions. In addition to the canonical examination to which these cases are subject, as in any ecclesiastical society, the Society of Saint Pius X seeks to entrust all accusations on this subject exclusively to the judicial authorities, in accordance with the requirements of local legislation.”</p><p>“The Society of Saint Pius X cooperates fully with all judicial investigations, leaving it to the competent authorities to evaluate in detail the circumstances of each case and to pronounce judgment in accordance with the laws in force. In particular, the Society of Saint Pius X relies on them to evaluate the possible responsibilities of each person (physical or institutional), to draw the judicial consequences, and to ensure they are applied.”</p><p>A better understanding of accusations facing SSPX priests in the U.S. could still be coming. The Kansas Bureau of Investigation released a report on child sexual abuse in local Catholic dioceses in 2023, and indicated it was still looking into accusations involving SSPX, as is the Kansas attorney general.</p><h3>How big is the Society of Saint Pius X?</h3><p>The U.S. headquarters for SSPX — which counts about 700 priests and an estimated 600,000 followers around the world — is in Missouri, and the group also oversees a large congregation in Kansas.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/5/23/23734334/clergy-sex-abuse-catholic-church-illinois-underreported-kwame-raoul-blase-cupich" target="_blank" >2023 Illinois attorney general</a> report on abusive Catholic clergy across the state didn’t mention SSPX.</p><p>The group runs a boarding school for boys in downstate Illinois, just south of Danville. It also oversees the Our Lady Immaculate Church at 410 W. Washington Blvd. in Oak Park, which the group bought in the early 1990s from a Presbyterian congregation. The group also has a priory in the Dunning neighborhood of Chicago in a building once owned by an order of nuns adjacent to St. Priscilla Parish.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div After spending some time in different locations, Welsh was assigned as a prior in Hampton from January 1986 until July 1993.”</p><p>While in that suburb of Melbourne, he repeatedly sexually assaulted Francis Ockerse, told Australian police that in 1991 he had dinner with an accuser who “made a vague allegation of sexual misconduct by Welsh and then promptly left the room without elaborating,” court records say.</p><p>Ockerse “did not pursue the matter because he did not have sufficient evidence about the allegation. not attending church was because Welsh had abused her.”</p><p>The young woman “then walked out and Ockerse said nothing,” and “nothing was ever done about this.” At least until 2007, when she said she was asked by another priest to give a “deposition” in an effort to “defrock” Welsh, court records show.</p><h3>Around 2008, victim’s parents learn of the abuse </h3><p>In or about 2008 “she told her hundreds of years.</p><p>The priests in the liturgy also began facing the congregation, rather than with their backs to the pews.</p><p>And, the council softened its teachings on — and relations with — other religions, including the Jewish faith that, over centuries, was often demonized by the church.</p><p>The Catholic News Service article says: “There are two notable texts from Vatican II that focus on religious liberty, ‘Dignitatis Humanae,’ which recognizes a civil right to religious freedom, and ‘Nostra Aetate,’ which encourages dialogue with non-Christian religions while recognizing elements of truth and holiness within them.”</p><p>SSPX not only continues to celebrate the traditional Latin liturgy, it “rejects modernity as the fruit of Satan’s work” and regards “non-Catholic entries.title: A Victorian bandstand gets ready for an encore while Jackson Park’s golden lady gets new clothes
entries.summary: <p>Some of the city’s best architecture is not only found around Chicago’s parks, but in them.</p><p>Yet for decades, the park district allowed many of its structures to fall into embarrassing disrepair.</p><p>Do I have to name names? For starters, how about places like the South Shore Cultural Center’s outdoor theater, which is a performance space that should be a civic asset. Instead, it’s been a <a class="Link" href="https://www.landmarks.org/preservation-programs/most-endangered-historic-places-in-illinois/outdoor-theater-at-the-south-shore-cultural-center-2025/" target="_blank" >decaying appendage</a> on the South Side of the former country club, 7059 S. South Shore Dr., seemingly since time immemorial.</p><p>But is the Chicago Park District starting to get its act together and do right by its architectural treasures? Two current projects give me some hope.</p><p>This summer, the district resumed its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/06/30/garfield-park-bandstand-restoration-chicago-park-district" target="_blank" >restoration of the nearly 130-year-old Garfield Park music bandstand</a> after a yearlong delay.</p><p>And the district also began the $1 million <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/03/31/jackson-park-gold-lady-million-planned-restoration" target="_blank" >anticipated fix-up</a> of the Gold Lady herself, Jackson Park’s gilded 24-foot tall Statue of the Republic.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-170000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Garfield Park Bandstand’s original copper roof will have to be placed as part of work happening there.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The work at the Garfield Park bandstand is particularly worthy of attention. With its marble base and copper roof, the structure, located in Garfield Park on Music Court Drive just east of Hamlin Avenue, is as unique and lovely a structure as you’ll see in this town.</p><p>It’s been under rehab for more than a year. The original $2.2 million scope of work included restoring the bandstand’s marble base, mosaic panels and electrical system.</p><p>The district stopped the project last year when workers discovered “hundreds of tiny pinholes in the copper roof,” according to a park spokesperson, that could make the mosaic dome underneath vulnerable to water damage.</p><p>But the project resumed this week. The copper roof — original to the building — will be replaced with one that matches what’s there now.</p><p>“Representative decorative copper elements, including the central finial, ridge scrolls and gabled dormers, were removed [last month] and delivered to a metalworking contractor that specializes in traditional metalworking techniques and historic ornamental fabrication,” park district spokesperson Irene Tostado said.</p><p>“Elements will be replicated exactly with a high degree of accuracy, craftsmanship and fidelity to the original historic design,” she said.</p><p>How much more will all this cost? Tostado said the district won't know until cost estimates are updated after a new assessment of the bandstand’s structural steel.</p><p>Workers are expected to start restoring the mosaic dome between August and November. The entire bandstand project should be done in December, Tostado said.</p><p>The bandstand, designed by Joseph Lyman Silsbee, was built in 1897. In its day, musicians would perform inside the Middle Eastern Revival structure, playing to crowds gathered around the circular Museum Court Drive and surrounding park land.</p><p>“The fact that [the bandstand is] so very ornamental and so lovely just kind of ties into the whole philosophy that everything that would be designed in these parks during that period would have that level of thought and expense and effort,” historian Julia Bachrach, author of “The City in a Garden: A History of Chicago’s Parks” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2025/06/30/garfield-park-bandstand-restoration-chicago-park-district" target="_blank" >told me last year.</a></p><p>If done right, it’ll be a great benefit to West Side park patrons and the city to have the bandstand restored and put back into service.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"
