The sculpture will be encapsulated in a shroud designed to protect the unfinished work and the artisans on the job from the elements.</p><p>The Gold Lady is a pared-down replica of original 65-foot golden gilded Statue of the Republic that stood in Jackson Park during the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition.</p><p>Parks and architecture have always been important to Chicago. And while the park district still has miles to go when it comes to restoring and rehabbing its key places and spaces, what’s happening in Garfield and Jackson are good signs. Keep it up.</p>

entries.title: What to know about the Rev. Michael Pfleger sex abuse investigation
entries.summary: <p>Earlier this month, the Archdiocese of Chicago launched an investigation into a decades-old child sexual abuse allegation against the Rev. Michael Pfleger, the longtime pastor of St. Sabina Church in Auburn Gresham.</p><p>It was the fifth such accusation brought against Pfleger in five years, and the investigation remains ongoing. The archdiocese found the four previous allegations to be unfounded. The latest allegation has brought renewed attention to Pfleger, whose decades of ministry and community activism have made him a prominent South Side figure. It has also prompted <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2026/07/13/saint-sabina-community-fateher-michael-pfleger-sex-abuse-allegation" target="_blank" >parish leaders</a> to call for changes to how the archdiocese handles allegations against priests.</p><p>Here’s what to know.</p><h3><b>What is the current allegation?</b></h3><p>The archdiocese <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/religion/2026/07/11/michael-pfleger-removed-st-sabina-church-sex-abuse-claim-blaise-cupich-catholic-church" target="_blank" >opened the latest investigation July 11</a>. It stems from an allegation that Pfleger sexually abused a girl who was a student at St. Sabina sometime between 1993 and 1995.</p><p>Pfleger, who has strongly denied the accusation, has been removed from active ministry while the Archdiocese of Chicago’s Independent Review Board investigates the claim.</p><p>The archdiocese has not released additional details about the allegation, but a spokesperson said this week that the investigation “remains ongoing [and] when we have updates, we will share them.”</p><p>The allegation was also reported to law enforcement, according to Cardinal Blase Cupich.</p><h3><b>Who is the Rev. Michael Pfleger?</b></h3><p>Pfleger, 77, has led St. Sabina Church since 1981, when he became the youngest pastor in the archdiocese.</p><p>Beyond his role as a priest, Pfleger is known for his anti-violence work and advocacy for racial and economic justice, making him a prominent civic figure beyond St. Sabina, a predominantly Black Catholic parish.</p><div class="Enhancement" Michael Pfleger, of Saint Sabina Church, speaks about allocating more resources and attention to the reduction of gun violence during a press conference to advance a Department of Gun Violence Reduction at City Hall in the Loop, Monday, June 22, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In addition to serving as a place of worship, St. Sabina has also been a hub for community organizing, youth programs and social justice efforts on the South Side.</p><p>Pfleger has often brought together religious leaders, activists and elected officials for public demonstrations and community initiatives. involving racial justice and violence prevention. </p><h3><b>What is the St. Sabina parish saying about this? </b></h3><p>St. Sabina leaders say they support investigating allegations of child sexual support of the Rev. Michael Pfleger, Friday, July 17, 2026.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Among their requests, the St. Sabina leaders are calling for:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-91644fd2-85f8-11f1-9bb7-7386b21a730a"><li>More transparency about investigation timelines and procedures</li><li>Quicker resolutions to cases</li><li>Independent review of allegations</li><li>A tiered suspension policy that would consider factors such as the age of an allegation and whether there is an ongoing risk to children</li></ul><p>In their letter, St. Sabina leaders said the current process “fails to differentiate circumstances where there is a need for immediate removal” because of ongoing risks to children “from circumstances where there is no reasonable concern that any alleged abuse is ongoing, but rather, the allegation is about abuse allegedly occurring decades ago.”</p><h3><b>Why does the archdiocese remove priests during investigations?</b></h3><p>The archdiocese's policy of removing priests from ministry while abuse allegations are investigated is rooted in a broader shift in how Catholic dioceses respond to accusations of clergy sexual abuse.</p><p>After decades of abuse scandals and criticism that church leaders failed to act quickly enough when allegations surfaced, the Archdiocese adopted a policy of removing accused priests from ministry while allegations are reviewed. The archdiocese says the action is a precautionary step intended to protect children, allow investigations to proceed without interference and maintain public trust.</p><p>In the early 1990s, the archdiocese began formalizing its investigations into abuse allegations, including removing priests from active ministry amid investigations.</p><p>In 2002, the archdiocese adopted the “one-strike” data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Cardinal Blase Cupich</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The archdiocese’s stated process is to report allegations of child sexual abuse to civil authorities, remove the accused priest from ministry and investigate the claim. The Independent Review Board then advises the archbishop on issues including whether there is a risk to children and whether a priest is fit to return.</p><p>St. Sabina leaders argue that the policy can unfairly damage an innocent priest’s reputation and their community before an investigation is complete, especially in cases involving decades-old accusations. The archdiocese maintains that temporary removal is necessary because of the church’s past failures to respond aggressively enough to abuse allegations.</p><p>“We are committed to following the same thorough and impartial process with everyone so accused,” a spokesperson for the Archdiocese of Chicago said. “Only by doing this can we be assured of fairness to all concerned.”</p><h3><b>What happened with Pfleger’s previous investigations?</b></h3><p>The first major investigation was in 2021, when two brothers alleged that Pfleger sexually abused them decades earlier when they were children. A third person later came forward with a similar allegation. Pfleger denied the accusations and was removed from ministry until months later, when Cupich reinstated Pfleger, saying the review board found there was insufficient reason to suspect Pfleger was guilty of the allegations.</p><p>In 2022, Pfleger was again removed from ministry after another child sexual abuse allegation dating back decades. Pfleger denied that allegation and, after another review, the review board said the allegation was not substantiated and Pfleger was reinstated.</p><p>St. Sabina leaders have pointed to those previous allegations, each of which the archdiocese deemed unfounded after it removed Pfleger for months at a time, as a reason they believe the process needs to change.</p><h3><b>What happens next?</b></h3><p>Pfleger remains removed from active ministry while the archdiocese’s investigation continues. The Independent Review Board will make a recommendation to Cupich about whether Pfleger can return to ministry.</p><p>Meanwhile, the Rev. Thulani Magwaza is serving as lead pastor of St. Sabina Parish.</p><p>St. Sabina leaders also have said they will give archdiocese officials time to review their concerns laid out in their letter before deciding on their next steps.</p>

entries.title: Canadian belugas faced ‘imminent risk’ of death before emergency flight to Chicago, marine park lawyer says
entries.summary: <p>The 30 beluga whales at Marineland Canada — including four now at Shedd Aquarium — were at “imminent risk” of being euthanized, a longtime advisor and lawyer for the shuttered aquatic park told the Chicago Sun-Times Wednesday.</p><p>“The bottom line is we have expended, since the beginning of COVID, all of our available reserves of funds to keep these animals alive and rehoused,” said Andrew Burns, speaking from Toronto, Canada.</p><p>Burns said no more whales are scheduled to leave Marineland this week, but that the goal is to remove all of them by Aug. 31.</p><div four bound for Shedd and two more to SeaWorld in San Antonio. In preparation for the move, water was partially drained from one of the pools, The Canadian Press reported.</p><p>The belugas were placed into slings, before being hoisted into metal containers. They were then trucked to Toronto Pearson Airport, where they were flown in a Boeing 777 to Chicago and San Antonio. For the safety of the whales, pilots had to be careful not to take off or land too steeply, according to The Canadian Press.</p><p>Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ontario, has been closed to the public since 2024. Opened in 1961, the sprawling park has for years faced accusations of mistreating animals. The number of visitors had dwindled through the years.</p><p>Late last year, the financially strapped park applied for permits to ship the whales to a theme park in China, but Canadian authorities denied the permits, determining the move wasn’t in the best interests of the whales. Marineland then told the Canadian government that the park had two options for the whales: relocation or euthanasia.</p><p>Burns said Wednesday that it costs about $1.5 million Canadian a month to care for the whales. That equates to about $1 million in U.S. currency.</p><p>Euthanasia was a “real, direct and imminent risk,” he said.</p><p>Some Canadian animal welfare advocates have described Marineland’s threat to euthanize the whales as a “manufactured crisis,” that essentially forced the Canadian government to approve sending the whales to four American and one Spanish aquarium.</p><p>The animal welfare advocates say they fear that the aquariums will now breed the Marineland whales, leading to more marine mammals living out their lives in captivity.</p><p>Burns said there are no birth control methods for beluga whales. “Animal welfare activists have very fixed ideological positions that do not relate in any way to the actual needs and experiences of animals,” Burns said. “So in demanding that they not breed, what they are doing is saying that these animals cannot be allowed to live in their normal social groupings." </p><p>He continued: “What they are really saying about Marineland is: Take family groups that have been together for decades and rip them apart and separate them so that families are broken apart. … I don’t agree with that at all."</p>

entries.title: Blackhawks reunite with Patrick Kane, signing him to two-year contract
entries.summary: <p>Patrick Kane is coming home — to his adopted home, not his actual home.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a> franchise legend reunited with the Hawks on Thursday, signing a two-year contract that carries an $8 million salary-cap hit after three weeks of free agency.</p><p>Kane, who grew up in Buffalo, had been deciding between the Hawks and his hometown Sabres. Hawks fans throughout the Chicago area and beyond will surely be thrilled about his eventual decision. </p><p>For general manager Kyle Davidson, the decision to bring back Kane after trading him to the Rangers three years ago represents a much-needed crowd-pleasing move — and a pivot from a previous stance.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">two more years of S H O W T I M E 🍿 <a href="https://t.co/ZTc6Xhi3ef">pic.twitter.com/ZTc6Xhi3ef</a></p>— Chicago Blackhawks (@NHLBlackhawks) <a href="https://x.com/NHLBlackhawks/status/2080275385023959434?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 23, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>"Day in and day out for 16 seasons, Patrick captivated the city of Chicago with his dazzling skill, creating some of the most memorable moments in Blackhawks history as he helped bring our storied franchise back to the pinnacle of our sport," Davidson said in a statement.</p><p>"He’s shown on countless occasions that he knows what it takes to win at the highest levels, and we couldn’t be prouder for Patrick to once again call the United Center home and continue to shine in Chicago’s brightest lights."</p><p>Kane is 37 years old now but remains a productive winger, recording 163 points in 189 games over the last three seasons with the Red Wings — including 57 points (41 of which were assists) in 67 games last season. The Wings, however, narrowly missed the playoffs all three years.</p><p>He has followed his former team fairly closely throughout his absence, praising the Hawks' "young, up-and-coming players" and Connor Bedard's ability to "make plays that other guys can't" to the Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2025/11/08/patrick-kane-blackhawks-red-wings-connor-bedard-jonathan-toews" target="_blank" >last November</a>.</p><p>Kane won't be able to immediately start the season next to Bedard while the latter recovers from shoulder surgery, but there's a good chance they play together eventually. Bedard made an impassioned pitch for Kane to return earlier this week, too.</p><p>Kane's contract contains a full no-movement clause, per the team. It also marks a massive raise — in other words, an obvious overpayment — for Kane, who made between $2.75 million and $4 million during each of his three seasons with the Wings. The Hawks can easily fit the $8 million cap hit for the next two years, though.</p><p>When Davidson dealt Kane and declined to re-sign Jonathan Toews in 2023, he explained that he wanted to give the Hawks' new generation — including Bedard — a blank slate to grow into leadership roles instead of deferring to franchise legends. And in 2024, he said he didn't "foresee" himself going back on that decision.</p><p>Evidently, Davidson believes enough of that leadership growth has occurred that Kane's return won't disrupt it. Toews' <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/06/19/jonathan-toews-retirement-blackhawks-jets-82-games" target="_blank" >retirement</a> might have also made this decision less complicated; it might've been messy to bring back just one of the two legends.</p><p><i>This story will be updated.</i></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wutklhy-l-k/" target="_blank" >Mexico seeks U.S. accountability in Chicago-area ICE death, 16 others</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wutklhy-l-u/" target="_blank" >Alma Campos</a></h5><p><b>Accountability push</b>: Mexico's government has begun taking legal action to seek accountability for the deaths of 17 of its citizens during U.S.Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations — 14 of them in ICE custody and three during other "arrest operations." Mexico President Claudia Sheinbaum has referred to these deaths as "homicides."</p><p><b>Midway Blitz tie</b>: Among those for whom Mexico is seeking accountability is Silverio Villegas González, who was shot and killed by an ICE agent during a traffic stop in suburban Franklin Park in September. Villegas González had lived in the United States since 2007and was the father of two young children.</p><p><b>Legal action</b>: Mexico officials have filed criminal complaints with state prosecutors in Illinois and elsewhere and plan to submit a complaint to the U.S. Department of Justice, seeking independent investigations into the deaths. The Mexican government also issued cease-and-desist letters directing U.S. detention centers to preserve records and called for a formal review by the United Nations Human Rights Council.</p><p><b>What will this do?</b>: Legal experts and immigration advocates say it's unclear whether U.S. authorities will cooperate with an investigation, but the process still could put political pressure on the United States to take action and potentially produce evidence that could be used in civil lawsuits. Mexico can’t compel the U.S. to investigate or collect evidence, experts say.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wutklhy-l-o/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>HEALTHCARE 🩺</h4><div class="Enhancement" women with long COVID experienced worse effects on their quality of life and cognitive functioning than men.</p><p><b>Common symptoms</b>: The research is based on evaluations of 2,329 patients who target="_blank" >Food brings this family together and one recipe reminds them of home</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wutklhy-l-th/" target="_blank" >Araceli Gómez-Aldana</a></h5><p>Food has been at the center of Teddy and Alexis Vejar’s lives since they were kids. They remember walking around their neighborhood in Morelia, Michoacán, where people would serve dinner out of their homes.</p><p>Today, the brothers own Jarabe in Little Italy. The restaurant opened in 2015 and prides itself on authentic Mexican cuisine. When they began developing their recipes, they focused on making things from scratch, like their grandmother did growing up. </p><p>Of all the dishes they grew up eating, one remains their favorite all these years later: Cochinita pibil. They serve it at their restaurant.</p><p>Teddy and Alexis have fond memories of living in Ukrainian Village when their dad began making homemade cochinita pibil for them and their extended family. Even today, the family gets together to eat the dish.</p><p>Cochinita pibil is a pulled pork dish. The pork is marinated in achiote paste and served with tortillas and pickled red onions. It’s considered one of Yucatán’s traditional dishes, and it’s a favorite celebration meal for the Vejar family.</p><p>WBEZ reporter Araceli Gómez-Aldana and photojournalist Manuel Martinez met up with the Vejars to learn more about what the dish means to them.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wutklhy-l-tk/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>WATCH: MAKING COCHINITA PIBIL ▶️</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/OazrsIWZC3Q?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Tastes from Home: Tortillas, togetherness and time well spent."></iframe> </div> </div></div><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><i>What Chicago restaurant feels like home to you? entries.title: First-place White Sox keep the line moving in second half — and Munetaka Murakami’s just getting warmed up
entries.summary: <p>ARLINGTON, Texas — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> passed a major test out of the All-Star break with two straight road series wins, no small feat for a team that went 19-28 while traveling during the first half of the season.</p><p>They did it with some <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/17/white-sox-toronto-braden-montgomery-murakami-derby" target="_blank" ><u>long ball</u></a> courtesy of Sam Antonacci and Colson Montgomery while taking two out of three in Toronto.</p><p>They did it with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/22/andrew-benintendi-white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>some small ball</u></a> in Texas, with Chase Meidroth and Andrew Benintendi combining for six singles driving in all their runs in a 4-2 rubber-match win at Texas.</p><p>They got big-time pitching performances from Davis Martin and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/19/sean-burke-white-sox-toronto-davis-martin-starting-pitchers" target="_blank" ><u>rising ace Sean Burke</u></a>, plus a bullpen that’s suddenly dealing shutdown stuff behind Grant Taylor, Bryan Hudson and a revitalized <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/21/jordan-hicks-white-sox-arm-slot" target="_blank" ><u>Jordan Hicks</u></a>.</p><p>And it’s hard not to wonder how it all could look for the stunning first-place Sox if Munetaka Murakami can regain his epically powerful first-half form.</p><p>The rookie sensation went 4-for-19 with two doubles, seven walks and eight strikeouts during his first road trip <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/10/white-sox-activate-munetaka-murakami-from-injured-list-option-jacob-gonzalez-to-charlotte" target="_blank" ><u>since returning</u></a> from the hamstring injury that derailed the spring dinger show that still landed him spots in the Home Run Derby and All-Star Game.</p><p>Murakami gave one a ride Wednesday night on a deep flyout at Globe Life Field, but he returned to Chicago still in search of his 21st home run, which would be his first since May 27. He’s confident it’s coming, even as the league looks for new ways to attack his prodigious swing.</p><p>“I think overall it’s getting better,” Murakami said via interpreter Kenzo Yagi. “I’ve been seeing the ball very clearly and I’m getting good at-bats. There are different pitchers coming in each and every day with different varieties of pitches. It’s always a learning curve on that as well.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-bd0000" things on the road. </p><p>“There was just more intent to be ready earlier,” Venable said. “Got the barrel to some balls. Didn't hit any out, but there were some really good swings in there.</p><p>“His presence is felt in the dugout, in the clubhouse and obviously on the field,” Venable added. “I think we saw in his absence that our group was still able to score a lot of runs… The positive things we're doing offensively are certainly driven by Mune, but not all driven by Mune. So even when he's not out there hitting homers every day, we find ways to score runs, because we're doing it really throughout the lineup.”</p><p>The Sox went 17-18 during the six weeks Murakami missed with a hamstring injury. They’ve gone 7-2 since he returned, behind a balanced attack getting steady production from Miguel Vargas (four doubles on the road trip with two RBI), Montgomery (team-leading 24 homers) and a rotating cast of nightly contributors.</p><p>“I think our offense is very multi-faceted,” Meidroth said after his 4-for-4 night Wednesday. “There are many ways to win a baseball game, which makes this team and lineup really special… It’s still July. Gotta take care of business.”</p><p>Murakami was just pleased to return to a squad defying the odds by sitting in first place with under two weeks remaining before the Aug. 3 trade deadline.</p><p>“As a team we are in a good condition,” he said. “Trying to win as much as possible so we can get first in the division, and hopefully in the World Series.</p><p>“We are going into games with good preparation. We have to continue to keep this up and the wins will come along,” Murakami said. “The whole team and atmosphere is concentrated on each and every single game like that. I think it shows out there every single day… We just have to keep continuing this grinding every single day and keep that success going.”</p><h3>On deck</h3><p><b>ASTROS AT SOX</b></p><p>Friday: Spencer Arrighetti (7-5, 4.34 ERA) vs. Davis Martin (9-5, 3.31), 6:40 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p>Saturday: Hunter Brown (1-1, 4.05) vs. Sean Burke (7-4, 3.20) 6:10 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p><p>Sunday: Ronel Blanco (0-0, 7.71) vs. Erick Fedde (5-6, 4.16), 1:10 p.m., CHSN, 1000-AM.</p>

entries.title: Blagojevich now seeking Trump clemency for former Indiana politician convicted in vote-buying scheme
entries.summary: <p>Former Illinois Gov. Rod Blagojevich is hoping to parlay his access to President Donald Trump into a moneymaking clemency ask for Frank Kollintzas,<b> </b>a former Indiana<b> </b>city<b> </b>councilman<b> </b>who allegedly fled to Greece<b> </b>after being convicted in a vote-buying scheme.</p><p>Trump in February 2025 issued a full and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/donald-trump/2025/02/10/trump-blagojevich-pardon-illinois-governor-sentence-commuted" >unconditional pardon to Blagojevich</a> after commuting his 14-year sentence for political corruption charges. Now, according to a federal lobbying disclosure form first reported by NBC News, Blagojevich is reporting income of $50,000 tied to lobbying activities for Kollintzas. <a class="Link" href="https://disclosurespreview.house.gov/ld/ldxmlrelease/2026/Q2/301893776.xml" target="_blank" ><u>According to the form</u></a>, Blagojevich is seeking presidential clemency on behalf of Kollintzas.</p><p>This isn't the first time Blagojevich's firm, RRB Strategies LLC, has filed disclosure forms seeking clemency. Last year, he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-corruption-trials/2025/12/31/blagojevich-clemency-anne-pramaggiore-comed-bribery" target="_blank" >tried to seek presidential clemency for former ComEd CEO Anne Pramaggiore</a>. The form says she was "wrongly prosecuted, wrongly convicted, and wrongly incarcerated." A federal appeals court ordered the release from prison of Pramaggiore and longtime lobbyist Michael McClain. It later formally wiped out the pair’s convictions, setting up the possibility of a new trial.</p><p>According to disclosures, Blagojevich reported three forms stemming from Pramaggiore's case — totaling income of $280,000 tied to lobbying for her. </p><p>Clemency lobbying is now a multi-million dollar industry — as the traditional pardon process coming from the Justice Department has shifted closer to the White House. Those seeking pardons from Trump, including attorneys and lobbyists, are using their White House connections to try to make a case for their clients, and people are indeed paying them top dollars to do so. Others are trying to get to Trump directly — including at Mar-a-Lago.</p><p>A federal jury found<b> </b>Kollintzas<b> </b>guilty<b> </b>in 2004<b> </b>of lying to a federal agent and converting funds of East Chicago, Indiana, where he served as councilman.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" wire fraud and lying to the FBI Sept. 5, 2003.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Christopher Smith/Post-Tribune</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>A judge later<b> </b>sentenced Kollintzas<b> </b>to more than 11 years<b> </b>in prison, writing that the charges related “to what can only be described [as] a frenzy of municipal improvements (new concrete and tree trimming) at city expense, but without legal authorization, in the weeks leading up to the 1999 primary election.”</p><p>Blagojevich spent eight years in federal prison before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2020/2/18/20792391/rod-blagojevich-trump-clemency-illinois-governor-patti" target="_blank" ><u>then-President Donald Trump commuted his sentence in February 2020</u></a>. Though an appellate court <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2015/7/21/18593248/blagojevich-and-family-disappointed-in-appellate-court-ruling" target="_blank" ><u>tossed five of Blagojevich’s 18 convictions in 2015</u></a>, federal prosecutors contend he remained convicted “of the same three charged shakedowns” for which he was first sentenced in 2011.</p><p>Those included his attempt to sell then-President-elect Barack Obama’s U.S. Senate seat, to shake down the CEO of Children’s Memorial Hospital for $25,000 in campaign contributions, and to hold up a bill to benefit the racetrack industry for $100,000 in campaign contributions.</p><p>Trump’s commutation did not undo Blagojevich’s convictions.</p><p>After signing the Blagojevich pardon in the Oval Office, along with a slew of other executive orders, Trump said, “It’s my honor to do it. I’ve watched him. He was set up by a lot of bad people, some of the same people that I had to deal with. He wasn’t quite as successful.”</p><p>Blagojevich, 69, met Trump when he was a contestant on Trump’s “Celebrity Apprentice” show in 2010, before his court case was fully resolved. Though he ended up being “fired,” Trump took a liking to the outgoing former governor.</p><p>The new business foray for Blagojevich is raising some eyebrows. Former Illinois House Republican Leader Jim Durkin, who served on the Special Investigation Committee that led to Blagojevich’s impeachment in 2008, said clemency for Kollintzas would cheat victims of the case — twice.</p><p>“It's one thing to erase the conviction, but it's worse when you erase the restitution where the people who were defrauded in all these cases that we're seeing receive nothing. They've been cheated twice by this individual. So I think that's really wrong,” Durkin said.</p><p>Durkin acknowledged that Blagojevich is now part of the cottage industry trying to curry favor with the president — an association he called “unsavory.”</p><p>“Victims still have rights in this country. So I would just say that if this is how the former governor is hanging his shingle, I guess he's got a couple years to do his magic,” Durkin said. “But I think it'll run out by the time the next administration comes in.”</p><p>Blagojevich did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p><i>Contributing: Jon Seidel</i></p>

entries.title: Girls from across Chicago become firefighters for a day
entries.summary: <p>For one day, 12-year-old Hannah Cole got to put on a helmet and learn what it’s like to be a Chicago firefighter.</p><p>Cole was one of dozens of girls who participated in the Chicago Fire Department’s "Firefighter for a Day" event Thursday morning at the Quinn Fire Academy, 558 W. De Koven St. The girls learned about fire safety, participated in drills and were able to spend time with members of the CFD.</p><p>“I consider them very important heroes,” Cole said.</p><p>Cole’s curiosity about what it’s like to be a firefighter and paramedic grew from watching firefighters on television. But after spending time with firefighters, many of whom were women, she said she could see herself becoming one in the future.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div entries.title: First look at Shedd Aquarium's newest beluga whales
entries.summary: <p>Shafts of sunlight angle into glistening turquoise water. Four beluga whales, in near-synchronized perfection, glide by, eyeing the cluster of visitors on the other side of a huge picture window.</p><p>One of those visitors is Karisa Tang, Shedd Aquarium’s vice president of animal health. Tang’s hand goes to her chest at the approach of these most graceful creatures — even though she’s seen Acadia, Lillooet, Osiris, and Sierra countless times before.</p><p>“That’s stunning in the sunlight,” Tang says during visit by the Sun-Times to the aquarium Thursday morning in an area — for the time being — closed to the public.</p><p>Two more Shedd scientists huddle nearby, eyes glued to computer screens as they monitor the health of the new arrivals.</p><p>So far, says Tang, the signs look good for the whales, which arrived just before dawn Tuesday from the now-shuttered Marineland, a once-popular tourist attraction in Niagara Falls, Ontario.</p><p>“We are seeing them foraging, engaging with the habitat, being curious, exploring together. … In the previous 48 hours, we’ve seen some really positive signs,” Tang said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-bd0000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Shedd Aquarium personnel watch the belugas swimming in their tank while monitoring the whales’ health on Thursday. Four beluga whales from Canada arrived at the Shedd Aquarium early Tuesday from Marineland, a now-shuttered tourist attraction in Niagara Falls, Ontario, Canada.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The new arrivals, all females and ranging in age from 21 to 27 (middle-aged in whale years), are for now being kept separate from Shedd’s other eight belugas. Different habitats of the 3-million-gallon Abbott Oceanarium are separated by metal gates.</p><p>“We are trying to introduce as few new things every day as possible,” Tang said. “Everything is going to be gradual — from what habitat they are in to how they are being fed to how they are interacting with people.”</p><p>For the record, their diet includes “restaurant quality” fish, squid and clams.</p><p>It’s probably fair to say that this week, the whales have had as much excitement as they can handle. On Monday, Shedd, Marineland and other marine mammal experts guided the belugas out of a partially drained pool and into cloth slings, before hoisting them into water-filled steel containers. The containers were then loaded into trucks bound for Toronto Pearson Airport, where a Qatar Airways Cargo Boeing 777 flew them to Chicago.</p><p>The flight took about an hour, said Tang, who was on board the wide-body jet. Imagine a first-class ticket with everything offered but a window seat. Staff ladled water onto exposed skin and offered soothing words to the six behemoths — the heaviest of the Chicago-bound whales weighing 2,400 pounds. Two more belugas on the same flight went on to SeaWorld in San Antonio. Staff monitored breathing rates and animal behavior. entries.title: How Jerry Seinfeld would diagnose the Sky’s All-Star problem
entries.summary: <p>In a famous “Seinfeld” scene, Jerry arrives at a car-rental counter with a reservation. The attendant tells him they have his reservation, but they ran out of cars. Seinfeld is perplexed: The whole purpose of the reservation is to keep the car there.</p><p>“I know why we have reservations,” the attendant tells him.</p><p>“I don’t think you do,” Seinfeld replies. “If you did, I’d have a car. See, you know how to take the reservations, you just don’t know how to hold the reservations. And that’s really the most important part.”</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> organization operates a lot like that car-rental place, as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/21/the-all-stars-the-sky-couldve-had-are-coming-to-chicago" >2026 All-Star weekend shows.</a></p><p>Many of the stars arriving in town this weekend — Kahleah Copper, Marina Mabrey, Courtney Williams and Angel Reese — have worn a Sky uniform before. All are now reaching new heights elsewhere.</p><p>Which just goes to show you that the Sky know how to take reservations — they know how to get talented players in the door. But since their 2021 championship, they haven't shown they know how to keep them.</p><p>Will this ever change? Can the Sky navigate the shift from an era in which top players often stayed with a single team for their entire careers — the way Courtney Vandersloot and Allie Quigley nearly did in Chicago — to one of much freer player movement?</p><p>Because once again, despite their losing record this season, the Sky have several young players with star potential.</p><p>Rickea Jackson, acquired from the Sparks in a steal of a deal, showed in four games before tearing her ACL that she can be the dynamic two-way forward teams need to contend.</p><p>Sydney Taylor, an undrafted rookie whom the Sky plucked from a Polish league, possesses <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/22/sydney-taylor-is-growing-fast-while-the-sky-repeat-old-mistakes" >another hugely valuable skill set</a>: She is a super-athletic gunner who creates her own shot too.</p><p>Kamilla Cardoso, the Sky’s No. 3 pick in the 2024 draft, has had stretches of absolute dominance inside.</p><p>All three are under team control through 2027 — Cardoso and Jackson are still on their rookie contracts, and Taylor can negotiate only with the Sky after this season.</p><p>But what happens after that? Will they want to sign long term?</p><p>We really don’t know. During training camp, Jackson said she would <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/04/22/will-this-time-be-different-sky-push-for-a-fresh-start" >run through a wall</a> for general manager Jeff Pagliocca and coach Tyler Marsh. Cardoso always calls the organization and coaching staff “amazing.”</p><p>But players often arrive saying all the right things — or genuinely believing them — then eventually decide their best career opportunities are elsewhere.</p><p>That’s been the pattern of the All-Star departures. The circumstances were different for Copper, Williams, Mabrey and Reese. But they all pointed to either 1) subpar resources 2) the whiplash of coaching changes or 3) both.</p><p>On the StudBudz livestream last season, Williams described the absurd scene after Sky practices: showering next to "randoms" at the public park district. She also couldn’t believe ownership wouldn’t spring for hotel rooms for players on game nights, despite the long commute back to their suburban housing.</p><p>Has the environment changed fundamentally since then? The evidence is mixed.</p><p>Resources have improved, as they have across the league. Players are now housed downtown, no longer practice at a park district and have access to a larger performance staff. But ownership’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/07/17/sky-push-practice-facility-opening-to-november-will-not-move-in-this-season" >mismanagement of the practice-facility timeline</a> undercuts some of that progress.</p><p>And as for stability in coaching? Marsh has gotten more runway than Teresa Weatherspoon did, but after what is likely to be a second season without a playoff appearance, whether he returns next season is anyone's guess.</p><p>Which brings us back to Seinfeld’s insight into the nature of reservations.</p><p>The Sky can feel good about having Jackson, Taylor and Cardoso under team control through 2027.</p><p>But control is not the same thing as commitment. A little more time does not guarantee trust. They still need to prove they can hold these players down. </p><p>That’s really the most important part.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: ‘My Way’ scores Seiya Suzuki’s latest hot streak: Are Cubs approaching ‘final curtain’ with free-agent-to-be?
entries.summary: <p>These days, when Seiya Suzuki steps to the plate for his first at-bat of a game at Wrigley Field, there’s a new song playing:</p><p>Frank Sinatra’s “My Way.”</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ right fielder took a listen at the suggestion of his trainer. He liked what he heard. He liked how it made him feel.</p><p>“It’s very calming,” Suzuki said through an interpreter Wednesday night. “Your first at-bat, when you’re walking up to hit, you get excited and you get your nerves going. It kind of settles everything down.”</p><p>It sure worked Wednesday, with Sinatra settling Suzuki in enough that he smacked his 17th homer of the season.</p><p>But are Suzuki’s days blasting balls into the bleachers numbered?</p><p>Like several of his Cubs teammates, Suzuki faces potential free agency on the other side of the 2026 season.</p><p>“And now, the end is near,” Ol’ Blue Eyes croons in the slugger’s new walk-up tune, “and so I face the final curtain.”</p><p>After five years on the North Side, it’s difficult to imagine this Cubs lineup without the 31-year-old Suzuki, especially as his latest hot streak powers a team seeking a deep October run.</p><p>“We know,” said center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong, asked what sort of offensive presence Suzuki is for the Cubs. “It’s been the last five years. It’s fun watching him hit a ball 110 miles an hour.</p><p>“When he’s producing and putting the ball in play hard, good things are usually happening for us. … When Seiya’s going, it’s really fun to watch. Usually, he can be a one-man wrecking crew.”</p><p>Right now, Suzuki is showing his ability to carry a lineup, with a 1.192 OPS and four homers during an ongoing 11-game on-base streak.</p><p>That sort of thing would seem like a hard piece of the puzzle to do without.</p><p>Jed Hoyer’s front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/22/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-jed-hoyer-pitching-nico-hoerner-buyers-nl-central-standings-brewers" >has the trade deadline to worry about</a> before thinking about the offseason. This Cubs team is trying to win the World Series with Suzuki this year and isn’t moving onto future championship chases just yet.</p><p>But it’s a decision that Hoyer & Co. will have to face at some point: After handing out big-money contract extensions to Crow-Armstrong and Nico Hoerner, as well as the $175 million free-agent deal to land Alex Bregman, last offseason, will there be enough room in the budget to bring Suzuki back?</p><p>Suzuki has been nothing short of terrific in his five seasons since arriving from Japan, with a 129 OPS-plus overall, making him 29 percent more productive than the average major league hitter. He’s been good enough this season to be approaching a career best in that category, at 132 after Wednesday’s homer.</p><p>His defense — at one point a source of consternation, given that infamous dropped fly ball at the end of the 2023 season — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/31/cubs-seiya-suzuki-throw-defense-right-field-free-agency-dansby-swanson" >has noticeably and dramatically improved</a>. While he’s maybe not a Gold Glover like many of his teammates, he’s closer to matching the defensive excellence found all over the field.</p><p>That combination figures to earn him a raise from the $19 million he’s making in the final season of his current contract.</p><p>But will the Cubs be willing to squeeze in another hefty salary?</p><p>Bregman is due $35 million in 2027. Dansby Swanson will make $28 million. Hoerner will be at nearly $24 million. Crow-Armstrong’s salary will jump from the sub-$1 million he’s making this year to north of $10 million.</p><p>And Suzuki is not the only free-agent-to-be on the current Cubs roster, with Shota Imanaga, Ian Happ and Jameson Taillon all slated to hit the market. There’s a mutual option on Matthew Boyd’s contract, potentially sending him to free agency, as well.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" >The Cubs need pitching now</a> as the trade deadline approaches. Boy, will they need pitching if 60 percent of the rotation leaves for free agency.</p><p>Could it all end with Suzuki wearing another uniform next season?</p><p>Should things play out that way, it would figure to be a sizable problem for the Cubs, who have spent five years witnessing the sort of impact he can make with his bat.</p><p>If these next few months do prove to be the end of Suzuki’s Cubs tenure, at least he, like the Chairman of the Board, can say:</p><p>“I did it my way.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: More than 24 states sue Trump administration over conditions placed on receiving disaster funding
entries.summary: <p>More than two dozen states on Thursday sued the Trump administration for requiring them to comply with election and immigration conditions as a condition of receiving billions of dollars in federal funding for disasters.</p><p>The lawsuit, filed in Rhode Island and challenging Federal Emergency Management Agency and Department of Homeland Security policies, argued the administration is requiring states to change their elections systems and help DHS with immigration enforcement. The conditions would also allow DHS to terminate grants at any time and for any reason.</p><p>“Once again, the Trump Administration is threatening to jeopardize public safety by unlawfully withholding billions in critical funding and once again, they won’t get away with it,” Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha said. </p><p>The states argue putting conditions on congressionally appropriated funding violates the Administrative Procedure Act and the U.S. Constitution’s spending clause. A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Illinois is among the states joining in the lawsuit.</p><p></p><p>The lawsuit is one of scores that have challenged the Trump administration over its repeated effort to browbeat mostly Democratic states into complying with its priorities to get billions of dollars in federal funding. The strategy has been used on everything from education funding to domestic violence grants to highway funding.</p><p>The courts have repeatedly found this strategy to be unlawful and unconstitutional. A ruling last year barred the administration from putting conditions on other FEMA funding, and a second ruling this year blocked the administration from redirecting DHS funding away from states not seen as supportive of its agenda.</p><p></p><p>The latest lawsuit argues the administration is attempting to apply some of the same conditions on 2026 funding, as it failed to do with funding last year.</p><p>Among the requirements being challenged in Thursday’s lawsuit is that states change their <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-executive-order-elections-mail-voting-b28c3425c1dc968cd0f57c61fb7a684e" target="_blank" >elections systems.</a> They must transition to paper-ballot systems, conduct a manual audit of voting systems, reconcile voters and verify the citizenship of every registered voter in the state’s voter databases.</p><p>If states fail to comply, they risk losing at least 20% of their Homeland Security Grant Program funding. That money is used to fund measures to protect citizens from cyberattacks and terrorism.</p><p><i>Contributing: Mary Norkol, Sun-Times</i></p>

entries.title: Springfield commission votes to release report on disgraced ex-state Rep. Harry Benton this month
entries.summary: <p>A Springfield commission voted Thursday to release a state government watchdog’s report on the conduct of a disgraced suburban lawmaker who resigned earlier this month after a series of sexual harassment allegations.</p><p>The legislative inspector general’s report on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/07/06/harry-benton-investigation-report-misconduct-illinois-legislature" target="_blank" ><u>ex-state Rep. Harry Benton</u></a>, D-Plainfield, is expected to be made public by the end of the month, following the unanimous vote from the General Assembly’s bipartisan Legislative Ethics Commission.</p><p>Calls for its release have grown in the wake of last week’s Chicago Tribune report that Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch learned of a previous allegation against Benton three years before the one that prompted Welch to remove Benton from their Democratic caucus in February.</p><p>This month, Welch made a point of noting that he demanded Benton’s resignation within “an hour” of receiving the report from Legislative Inspector General Mike McCuskey on the sealed allegations against the representative.</p><p>Benton <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/07/03/plainfield-state-rep-harry-benton-resigns-amid-allegations-of-misconduct" >stepped down</a> July 3, but hasn’t addressed the allegations — or given up his $72,000-per-year elected post as Wheatland Township highway commissioner.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a But in 2023, Welch’s office waited months to probe a separate complaint against Benton and didn’t take any meaningful action.</p><p>Welch, who took the speaker’s gavel in the wake of now-federally convicted Michael Madigan in 2021, later made a Benton complainant uncomfortable with his use of heart-eye faces and other emojis in response to social media posts, she told the Tribune.</p><p>"The Legislative Inspector General’s independent investigation into former Representative Benton provides a full and accurate account of the steps my office took to support those who came forward," Welch said in a statement Wednesday. "My colleagues in the House Democratic Caucus and I have been clear that the report should be released while taking any necessary steps to protect the privacy and dignity of the innocent people who spoke out. Today’s vote is a positive step for accountability and transparency, and I look forward to the full report being released this month.”</p><p>Republicans have painted the harassment scandal as a repeat of history in Democratic-controlled Springfield, where Madigan’s reign began crumbling after revelations of mishandled harassment complaints within his political organization.</p><p>“When Speaker Welch first took the gavel, he promised a ‘new day,’” the House Republican Organization said in a statement. “Yet despite those promises of reform, it is becoming increasingly clear that they are ringing hollow.”</p><p>“Thank you to the members of the Legislative Ethics Commission for doing the right thing: transparency is key for us to move forward, understand how we can improve, and to demand accountability for those who failed to uphold the integrity of our chamber,” House Minority Leader Tony McCombie, R-Savanna, said in a statement. “Unfortunately, we may never know what happened before this report due to the silence of leaders who have repeatedly chosen politics over principles.”</p><p>It all poses the greatest threat yet to Welch’s hold on the gavel. The House Democratic Women’s Caucus issued a statement Wednesday calling for the report’s release and more stringent anti-harassment measures from Welch.</p><p>“When anyone reports harassment or abuse, leadership must act swiftly to investigate the matter and support the person who came forward,” caucus members wrote. “Simply referring a complainant to the Legislative Inspector General is insufficient — and if the person who reported the harassment chooses not to pursue that route, leadership must take further action to protect others in the workplace.”</p><p>At an unrelated news conference Wednesday, Gov. JB Pritzker left it up to House members to “make a decision about whether he should be their leader going forward.”</p><p>“The speaker has a responsibility to be utterly and completely transparent about the situation, to make sure that he is letting the public know, as well as, in particular, his members, know exactly what happened, and to the extent that he made mistakes, to own up to those mistakes,” Pritzker said.</p><p>Benton and the complainant will be able to review the report, suggest redactions and provide responses to the commission, which “intends to have this process completed by July 31.”</p>

entries.title: ESPN's Holly Rowe continues telling WNBA's stories at All-Star Game in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>Bad weather in the Northeast last Saturday canceled seemingly every flight out of New York. Ryan Ruocco and Rebecca Lobo, ESPN’s lead tandem for WNBA games, weren’t going to be able to join sideline reporter Holly Rowe in Dallas for a noon tipoff Sunday on ABC.</p><p>Rodney Vaughn, ESPN’s coordinating producer for WNBA coverage, had to figure out a solution. For a play-by-play replacement, he flew in White Sox TV voice John Schriffen from Las Vegas, where he was calling NBA Summer League games. And for an analyst, Vaughn felt he didn’t need to fly in anyone.</p><p>“We said, ‘We’ve got Holly Rowe,’ ” Vaughn said. “There’s not going to be another analyst that knows this league that could come in and do something in a one-game situation better than Holly. We felt that she could help carry the telecast and wouldn’t need a third person.”</p><p>So Rowe called the Sparks-Wings game as a first-time national WNBA analyst. She had been an analyst for college basketball, the NBA’s Jazz and the WNBA’s Utah Starzz, but never on less than 24 hours of notice.</p><p>“I was super nervous,” Rowe said. “I had butterflies in my chest.”</p><p>Wings veteran Alysha Clark told Rowe what former WNBA star Tina Thompson told her when she joined the league: “Trust the work.”</p><p>With 30 years of experience covering the WNBA, Rowe did just that.</p><p>“Holly was great,” Vaughn said. “Holly could step into an analyst chair and still drop nuggets, like [Wings guard] Arike Ogunbowale’s brother being a football player. On a replay, she’s describing how Arike’s cradling the ball like an NFL running back coming through the lane. That’s only because Holly is flexible enough where she could adapt that story into the role of an analyst.”</p><p>Rowe won’t have to be so nimble Saturday, when she’ll return to the sideline for ABC’s broadcast of the 30th WNBA All-Star Game at 7:30 p.m. at the United Center. She’ll be joined by Ruocco and Lobo, who don’t expect any problems flying to Chicago.</p><p>“She shouldn’t even be identified as just a sideline reporter,” Lobo said. “What she brings to a game is a lot more than what a typical sideline reporter would bring.”</p><p>Indeed she does, and it’s evident in her interviews. Players and coaches enjoy talking with her. Even when she’s on a college football sideline for ESPN’s biggest games, Rowe can unwind the most wound-up coaches. That comes from the relationships she has developed, and it’s displayed most with WNBA players.</p><p>“One of the biggest things is, I show up,” she said. “I show up to practices. I show up to press conferences. If someone’s having an event, I show up. I want them to know how deeply invested in them and this game I am. I make sure that they know I’m shining a light on them in every possible way. I think they appreciate that.”</p><p>“Part of that, too, is trust. They know that I’m going to have their best interests. I do ask hard questions when I need to. But I think they know I’m going to do it in the most respectful way.”</p><p>Despite her credentials, Rowe said she’s the one person on the broadcast who is never guaranteed airtime unless she sells the producer on a story. One story she has lined up for Saturday is a conversation with Tempo All-Star and former Sky guard Marina Mabrey, who’s working with an “energy coach” to ensure her fiery manner doesn’t hurt her team.</p><p>Though she’s prepared for countless possibilities, Rowe wants most of her contributions to the broadcast coming live, whether it’s information she’s sharing or passing on to Ruocco and Lobo.</p><p>“My job is access and observation,” Rowe said. “I am down there to tell fans something that they can’t see at home. So I want 70% to 80% of my content to be something that I have observed and only I could observe because of where I’m at. I need to be the eyes and ears of the fan.”</p><p>Rowe has been involved with the WNBA since its inception. Just to be a part of it, she began by pulling cables and serving as a stage manager for the Starzz, who are now the Aces.</p><p>She worked her way to the top telling the stories of others.</p><p>“It’s never been about Holly,” Lobo said. “She’s motivated completely by these athletes having interesting stories to tell, and I think sometimes she feels like, ‘If I don’t tell them, they’re never going to get told.’ And I think that’s why she’s better than anyone else at that.”</p><h3><b>WNBA ALL-STAR GAME</b></h3><p><b>The facts:</b> 7:30 p.m. Saturday at United Center, ABC 7.</p><p><b>Pregame show:</b> “WNBA Countdown” at 7 p.m.</p><p><b>Broadcast highlights:</b> Coaches Cynthia Cooper and Teresa Weatherspoon and select players will wear microphones during the game.</p><div entries.title: CTU and SEIU back different candidates for school board president, widening rift between staff unions
entries.summary: <p>In yet another public break with the politically powerful Chicago Teachers Union, the second-biggest union representing Chicago public school workers announced Thursday that it is endorsing Jessica Biggs in the race for the first elected school board president.</p><p>By declining to back the CTU’s pick and getting behind a candidate the teachers union slammed on social media hours earlier, the Service Employees International Union continues to drift apart from a union that was once its close ally.</p><p>Now, as parents head to the polls in November, they might be torn over whether to support the candidate recommended by their child’s teacher wearing the red CTU T-shirt, or the one supported by their special education classroom aide and bus monitor wearing SEIU purple.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/07/16/spending-in-chicago-school-board-election-exceeds-1-6-million-as-limits-lift-in-race-for-board-president" >Both unions have considerable financial resources</a>, a state and local presence and tens of thousands of workers who can knock on doors. SEIU represents about 16,500 CPS employees and more than 160,000 workers across the state. CTU has 30,000 CPS members and its president, Stacy Davis Gates, also leads the Illinois Federation of Teachers with more than 100,000 members.</p><p>In both of these unions, members can choose to deduct money from their paychecks to go to political committees, in addition to their dues to support union activities.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/07/13/ctu-endorses-15-school-board-candidates-throwing-weight-behind-incumbents-mayoral-picks" >The CTU has endorsed</a> their former political director, Hilario Dominguez, in the race for school board president. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/05/22/meet-the-candidates-for-chicagos-first-ever-elected-school-board-president" >The other candidates</a> are Jennifer Custer, a current school board member and former educator; Victor Henderson, an attorney and board member of the charter operator Urban Prep; and Sendhil Revuluri, a former math teacher appointed to serve on the school board by former Mayor Lori Lightfoot.</p><p>In a press release, SEIU officials praised Biggs, a current school board member and former CPS principal who is now working for the nonprofit Southwest Organizing Project. They described her as a “builder of coalitions” and someone who has worked in “classrooms, hallways and communities.”</p><p>“She doesn’t just talk about equity, she’s built it, school by school and block by block on the Southwest Side,” said Dian Palmer, the president of SEIU Local 73, the chapter that represents most of SEIU’s CPS employees.</p><p>The SEIU and the CTU used to work together to protest budget cuts, school closings and other actions that affected workers. SEIU was one of the biggest backers of CTU-organizer-turned-mayoral-candidate Brandon Johnson, and its related PACs contributed more than $4.6 million to his campaign.</p><p>But a rift formed after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2024/12/03/chicago-teachers-union-narrows-contract-demands-in-negotiations-with-cps" >CTU attempted to get some of SEIU’s members reclassified</a> so they would be under CTU. SEIU officials accused the CTU of raiding its members.</p><p>Ever since, the two unions have stood on opposite sides of several issues, including in the debate last year over how the school district should balance its budget.</p><p>Their interests sometimes still align. SEIU and CTU endorsed four of the same school board candidates. Also, workers from both unions are losing their jobs due to CPS’ budget deficit and subsequent cuts, and the unions have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/05/13/as-cps-cuts-staff-to-plug-deficit-educator-unions-and-school-board-members-press-for-more-state-funding" >lobbied state lawmakers to spend more on education</a>.</p><p>The CTU, in its Wednesday social media post, characterized Biggs as the candidate supported by the “architects of the destruction of Chicago’s Public Schools.” <a class="Link" href="https://www.ctulocal1.org/posts/the-architects-of-the-destruction-of-chicagos-public-schools-have-found-their-candidate/" target="_blank" >The teachers union pointed to donations</a> made to Biggs’ campaign by supporters and appointees of former Mayor Rahm Emanuel, whom the CTU despises for closing 50 schools.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://x.com/biggs4chicago/status/2080044820714656255" target="_blank" >Biggs responded on social media</a> by saying that she spoke out as a CPS principal against the privatization of custodial services and special education budget cuts while Emanuel was in office.</p><p>“I’m proud of my progressive record, both in practice and in the Board room,” she wrote in the post. “And, I’m eager to fight for what’s in the best interest of Chicago’s students, families, and educators and CPS staff alike.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div entries.title: Pritzker signs law designating July 25 as Emmett Till Day in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>On what would've been Emmett Till's 85th birthday, Illinois will observe its first official day in his honor.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker signed a bill Thursday morning designating July 25 as a statewide day of reflection and remembrance of Emmett and his mother, Mamie Till-Mobley. </p><p>Till lived on Chicago's South Side. The Black teen was 14 when he was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/emmett-till" >lynched on a trip to Mississippi </a>in 1955.</p><p>“In Illinois, we understand that we cannot build a more just future if we are unwilling to confront the injustices of our past,” Pritzker said at a news conference at Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ, where Till's funeral was held in 1955 — a funeral at which his mother insisted on an open casket, saying: "Let the people see what they did to my boy."</p><p>“This legislation ensures that Emmett Till and his mother Mamie Till-Mobley will never be forgotten, their legacy will continue to challenge us to be better, and their example will continue to inspire us to build a state and a nation that lives up to its highest ideals," Pritzker said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b50000" name="image-b50000"></a> <picture He has been memorialized in scholarships for local youth, the names of roads and community centers, and nationally recognized monuments across the state. In 2023, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2023/8/1/23815572/emmett-till-national-monument-roberts-temple-church" target="_blank" >Roberts Temple was made a national landmark</a> by President Joe Biden.</p><p>"While we are here today to reflect, we also understand that our reflection is only as useful as the action it inspires. Our mandate as Americans is to learn from the past so that we can transform our future," Pritzker said. "Every generation inherits that same responsibility to pick up the baton, to use the courage and sacrifice of the previous generation to leave a better world for the next one."</p><p>Till was lynched Aug. 28, 1955, while visiting relatives in Mississippi. A woman named <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/8/22/18385147/emmett-till-murder-did-carolyn-bryant-donham-recant-the-quote-wasn-t-recorded" target="_blank" >Carolyn Bryant Donham</a> accused him of making improper advances at a grocery store where she was working in the small community of Money.</p><p>His death <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2022/3/29/23002462/biden-signs-emmett-till-anti-lynching-bill-till-rep-bobby-rush-d-ill-chief-house-sponsor" target="_blank" >became a turning point in civil rights history</a>, in part after a key decision by his mother. Mamie Till-Mobley insisted on an open casket for his funeral at Roberts Temple so the world could see Till’s mutilated body and witness the deadly results of race-based violence.</p><p>"‘Let the people see what they did to my boy," she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-200000" "Thousands of black people were lynched and murdered in terror campaigns intended to strike fear and maintain control. But Mamie Till-Mobley forced our nation to face the extreme cruelty of the racism that had taken away her son and so many others." </p><p>Elected officials and community members on Thursday stressed the importance of celebrating the latest step in honoring Till's life and legacy while acknowledging there's still a long way to go.</p><p>"While we've made extraordinary progress in our pursuit of a more perfect union, too many of the injustices that took Emmett Till's life away remain," said state Sen. Elgie R. Sims, Jr., D-Chicago.</p><p>"We're still fighting the reality and the sting of racism. We're still fighting inequity in education, healthcare and economic opportunities. We're still fighting for a justice system that recognizes the humanity that fails to recognize the humanity and dignity of every person," Sims added.</p><p>"Every policy that advances justice, passed, every bill signed, every monument built, is in the spirit of the legacy of accountability and progress." Pritzker said. "We understand here in Illinois that we cannot build a more just future if we are unwilling to confront the injustices that have been committed in our past."</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/emmett-till" >READ: More about Emmett Till and the aftermath of his death</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Heisman Trophy runner-up Diego Pavia cut by Ravens
entries.summary: <p>OWINGS MILLS, Md. — The Baltimore Ravens waived quarterback Diego Pavia on Thursday, just a day before rookies were to report to training camp.</p><p>Pavia, the Heisman Trophy runner-up last season at Vanderbilt, signed as an undrafted free agent in April.</p><p>He had hoped to compete for the third quarterback spot behind two-time MVP Lamar Jackson and veteran Tyler Huntley. Skylar Thompson and Joe Fagnano will vie for that spot.</p><p>Pavia led Vanderbilt to the first 10-win season in program history, passing for 3,539 yards and 29 touchdowns. But his 5-foot-10 stature was a major question among scouts on whether Pavia could transfer that success to the NFL.</p><p>Veteran center Ethan Pocic took Pavia's place on the 90-player roster.<br></p>

entries.title: Small businesses took on debt, raised prices to cope with tariffs
entries.summary: <p>Tariffs imposed last year drove small-business owners to take on new debt, tap into retirement savings and raise prices, among other measures, according to a national survey released this week. </p><p>Many businesses experienced challenges beyond the cost of tariffs, said national grassroots group We Pay the Tariffs in a survey of 241 businesses in 40 states, including six in Illinois.</p><p>In Chicago, yarn store Dropped Stitch, incense maker Genieco and furniture seller Moderne Living participated in the survey.</p><p>Sporting goods maker Boombah based in Yorkville, west of Chicago, delayed expansion and new product development and froze hiring.</p><p>“Tariffs must often be paid up front, creating a significant cash flow burden,” Moderne Living Chief Operating Officer Rae Muranski said in the report. “This ties up working capital long before customer payments are received, making it especially difficult for small businesses to fund operations, invest in growth and remain competitive."</p><p>We Pay the Tariffs released its report days after President Donald Trump on Monday threatened 50% tariffs on most <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-canada-50-tariff-autos-alcohol-cheese-ca268ef24992b16695954c4c2e5eae6a" target="_blank" ><u>Canadian goods</u></a> starting in August. The move could unleash a new wave of economic chaos, with risks of higher inflation and further fraying of relations between the two nations.</p><p>The U.S. announced Thursday it will impose taxes of 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 countries accounting for 99% of U.S. imports, charging that they have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.</p><p>New tariffs “will only deepen the debt, extend the uncertainty and push more of these businesses toward the edge,” Dan Anthony, executive director of We Pay the Tariffs, said in a news release.</p><p>Its survey found that 45% of respondents took on new debt, and 40% tapped personal savings, such as retirement funds, in response to tariffs.</p><p>When asked how their business had fared over the last year, 57% of respondents said it had declined, and four in five of those respondents named tariffs as a major factor.</p><p>Nearly 30% of businesses laid off workers, and 56% delayed or canceled planned investments and new product development as a result of tariffs.</p><p>To absorb added costs, 83% of respondents raised prices, and 85% saw reduced profit margins.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/02/20/supreme-court-trump-sweeping-tariffs-john-roberts-economic-agenda" target="_blank" ><u>U.S. Supreme Court</u></a> in February ruled that some tariffs imposed by Trump last year were unconstitutional. In March, the U.S. Court of International Trade determined that companies subjected to tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act were entitled to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/03/05/illinois-businesses-tariff-refunds-federal-court-trade" target="_blank" ><u>refunds</u></a>.</p><p>We Pay the Tariffs’ survey was open April 24 to July 15; most businesses responded in April and May. Some had applied for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2026/04/21/illinois-businesses-mixed-results-tariff-refund-process" target="_blank" ><u>tariff refunds</u></a>, and others were still navigating a process that requires extensive documentation.</p><p>“For many, the claims process created additional hurdles, and even successful applicants incurred new administrative costs on top of the tariffs they had already paid,” said the We Pay the Tariffs report.</p><p>Many businesses would use tariff refunds as a lifeline, with 27% of survey respondents planning to use them to avoid closing, and 53% expecting to pay off debt.</p><p>“We've accumulated massive debt due to the tariffs, so if refunded, it would go to pay down that debt to help us remain in business,” said Kelly Weinberger, founder of jewelry company WorldFinds in Westmont, west of Chicago, in the report.</p><p>In May, Marla Showfer, owner of gift business the Winding Road in west suburban St. Charles, applied for tariff refunds totaling more than $18,000. So far, she has received one refund of nearly $3,700 and is waiting for the others. Meanwhile, the Winding Road is still paying 19% tariffs on handbags and goods from Indonesia.</p><p>Hannah Wilson, owner of the Dropped Stitch, 1524 W. Bryn Mawr Ave. in Edgewater, had paid nearly $1,500 in duties and fees in the last year by the end of April.</p><p>“I haven’t tallied extra expenses in terms of my vendors raising their wholesale prices for items that they themselves imported, but I’d estimate it’s at least that much again,” Wilson said in an email. “I know it's peanuts compared to the millions of dollars other companies are spending, but it’s significant in terms of my little 600-square-foot shop.”</p><p><i>Contributing: AP</i></p>
